## 1182. Schema.org Interconnected `@graph` URI Invariant (Harvested from spatie/schema-org & Yoast SEO)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [spatie/schema-org](https://github.com/spatie/schema-org) (`src/Graph.php`, SHA: `85af98461b7e899a8f5fd745331fac6ae5c745d9`) and Yoast SEO Schema Graph architecture.  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Google Search Central Structured Data documentation and Schema.org `@graph` specifications.

**RULE**:
Search-engine-facing structured data (JSON-LD) MUST NEVER be output as multiple disconnected top-level `<script type="application/ld+json">` blocks containing unlinked entities. Instead, all structured data for a document MUST be emitted in a single unified `<script type="application/ld+json">` tag containing an `@graph` array. Each entity (Organization, WebSite, WebPage, Article, Author, BreadcrumbList) MUST possess a deterministic, fully-qualified URI as its `@id` (e.g. `https://example.com/#organization`, `https://example.com/#website`) and reference related entities via `{"@id": "..."}` pointers.

**WHY**:
Google's Knowledge Graph parser extracts entity relationships, not isolated dictionaries. When a page serves four separate disconnected JSON-LD scripts:
- Script 1: `Organization`
- Script 2: `WebSite`
- Script 3: `Article`
- Script 4: `BreadcrumbList`

The search crawler cannot deterministically deduce that the `Article` was authored by the `Person`, published by the `Organization`, hosted on the `WebSite`, and categorized by the `BreadcrumbList`. Emitting an integrated `@graph` array with explicit URI references eliminates entity ambiguity, establishes verified publisher provenance, and significantly boosts eligibility for Google Knowledge Graph, Top Stories carousels, and rich result cards.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- Every page providing structured schema markup for articles, products, organizations, recipes, software applications, and FAQs.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```html
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@graph": [
    {
      "@type": "Organization",
      "@id": "https://example.com/#organization",
      "name": "Enterprise Core Systems",
      "url": "https://example.com",
      "logo": {
        "@type": "ImageObject",
        "@id": "https://example.com/#logo",
        "url": "https://example.com/logo.png",
        "caption": "Enterprise Core Systems Logo"
      }
    },
    {
      "@type": "WebSite",
      "@id": "https://example.com/#website",
      "url": "https://example.com",
      "name": "Enterprise Core Systems",
      "publisher": {
        "@id": "https://example.com/#organization"
      }
    },
    {
      "@type": "WebPage",
      "@id": "https://example.com/seo-guide/#webpage",
      "url": "https://example.com/seo-guide/",
      "name": "Comprehensive Technical SEO Architecture Guide",
      "isPartOf": {
        "@id": "https://example.com/#website"
      },
      "breadcrumb": {
        "@id": "https://example.com/seo-guide/#breadcrumb"
      }
    },
    {
      "@type": "BreadcrumbList",
      "@id": "https://example.com/seo-guide/#breadcrumb",
      "itemListElement": [
        {
          "@type": "ListItem",
          "position": 1,
          "name": "Home",
          "item": "https://example.com"
        },
        {
          "@type": "ListItem",
          "position": 2,
          "name": "SEO Architecture Guide",
          "item": "https://example.com/seo-guide/"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "@type": "Article",
      "@id": "https://example.com/seo-guide/#article",
      "isPartOf": {
        "@id": "https://example.com/seo-guide/#webpage"
      },
      "headline": "Comprehensive Technical SEO Architecture Guide",
      "publisher": {
        "@id": "https://example.com/#organization"
      },
      "mainEntityOfPage": "https://example.com/seo-guide/"
    }
  ]
}
</script>
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```html
<!-- ANTI-PATTERN: Multiple isolated, disconnected JSON-LD tags -->
<script type="application/ld+json">
  {"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "Article", "headline": "SEO Guide"}
</script>
<script type="application/ld+json">
  {"@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "Organization", "name": "Company"}
</script>
<!-- Entities are disjointed, no @id relationships, zero Knowledge Graph linkage -->
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1. Run Google Rich Results Test or Schema Validator CLI: assert valid graph resolution and no unlinked root entities.
2. In unit tests, validate JSON schema output parses into an `@graph` array where every entity contains a unique `@id`.

**RULE**:  
> **MUST** reserve a contiguous range of token IDs exclusively for image‑related tokens and **MUST NOT** reuse any of those IDs for textual tokens.  

**WHY**:  
Cross‑attention between image and text embeddings relies on token‑ID discrimination. Overlap causes the decoder to misinterpret image context as text, leading to hallucinations or silent failures.  

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
All multimodal models that embed visual tokens into a shared vocabulary, regardless of language or framework.  

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# configuration.ZDTaichu5_0_Config

    "img_start_token_id": 248055,
    "img_context_token_id": 248056,
    "img_end_token_id": 248057,
}
# Ensure no overlap with text vocab
assert all(id not in text_vocab for id in image_token_ids.values())
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# BAD: Reusing text token ID for image start
img_start_token_id = 50256  # same as BOS in GPT‑like vocab
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:  
Run a unit test that enumerates all token IDs in the tokenizer and verifies that the image token set is disjoint from the text vocab.

```python
    image = image.resize((target_size, target_size), Image.BILINEAR)
    return image
```

**RULE**:  
A model’s tokenizer must assign a unique integer ID to every special token across all modalities, and the model configuration must reference those IDs exactly.

**WHY**:  
Duplicate IDs cause ambiguous token interpretation, leading to incorrect embeddings, mis‑aligned attention, and catastrophic generation failures (e.g., `<|image_pad|>` being treated as `<|video_pad|>`).

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
During tokenizer construction, model configuration generation, and any downstream merging logic (processor, inference pipeline).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# tokenizer_config.json
{
  "image_token_id": 248056,
  "video_token_id": 248057,
  "audio_bos_token_id": 248058,
  "audio_eos_token_id": 248059,
  "audio_token_id": 248060,
  "pad_token_id": 248061,
  "eos_token_id": 248044
}
# model config references the same IDs
"image_token_id": 248056,
"video_token_id": 248057,
"audio_bos_token_id": 248058,
"audio_eos_token_id": 248059,
"audio_token_id": 248060,
"pad_token_id": 248061,
"eos_token_id": 248044
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# BAD: duplicate ID
"image_token_id": 248056,
"video_token_id": 248056,   # collision
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:  
Run a unit test that loads both tokenizer and model config, then asserts `set(tokenizer.special_tokens_ids) == set(model_config.special_token_ids)`.

**RULE**:  
The sequence of `layer_types` in the text configuration must match the declared `num_hidden_layers`; each entry must be a valid attention type (`linear_attention` or `full_attention`).

**WHY**:  
A mismatch leads to out‑of‑range indexing during forward passes, raising `IndexError` or silently skipping layers, which corrupts the output distribution.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
During model initialization; any script that programmatically modifies `layer_types`.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python

  "linear_attention", "linear_attention", "linear_attention", "full_attention",
  # ... 24 more entries, total 32
]
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

"layer_types": ["linear_attention", "full_attention"]  # only 2 layers
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:  
A linter rule that parses `layer_types` and checks `len(layer_types) == num_hidden_layers` and that each element is in the allowed set.

## 1189. Environment-Aware Non-Production Indexing Quarantine Invariant (Harvested from harlan-zw/nuxt-seo)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [harlan-zw/nuxt-seo](https://github.com/harlan-zw/nuxt-seo) (`packages/site-config/src/context.ts` & `@nuxtjs/seo`, SHA: `87700ddb4fbb4d1a4835e684b3c6b9f0bf978787`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Nuxt Site Config automated environment detection and quarantine cascades.

**RULE**:
Every web application, modern framework layout, and edge proxy MUST implement an immutable environment-aware indexing quarantine:
1. Unless `NODE_ENV === 'production'` AND `SITE_INDEXABLE === true` on an explicitly authorized production domain, the application MUST systematically emit:
   - `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">` in the HTML `<head>`.
   - HTTP Header `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow, noarchive`.
   - Dynamic `/robots.txt` with `User-agent: *\nDisallow: /`.
2. Public sitemap generation endpoints MUST return HTTP 404 or an empty URL set when requested in non-production environments.
3. Preview deploys (e.g. Vercel `*.vercel.app`, Netlify `*.netlify.app`, Cloudflare Pages `*.pages.dev`, staging Kubernetes clusters) MUST NEVER inherit production crawl permissions.

**WHY**:
Accidental staging and preview deployment indexation is one of the most destructive and common failure modes in modern continuous deployment. When search crawlers index preview branches, staging servers, or development endpoints:
- The staging domain creates massive duplicate content competition against the canonical production domain.
- Googlebot frequently splits ranking equity between staging and production, leading to organic traffic collapse.
- Sensitive pre-release features, internal staging URLs, and unreleased content leak into public search engine results.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- All continuous deployment setups, CI/CD preview branches, staging environments, QA servers, and multi-tenant platforms.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
// Production Quarantine Invariant Middleware
interface EnvironmentConfig {
  isProduction: boolean;
  siteUrl: string;
  isIndexable: boolean;
}

export function resolveIndexingPolicy(env: EnvironmentConfig): {
  robotsMeta: string;
  robotsHeader: string;
  disallowAll: boolean;
} {
  // RULE 1189: Quarantine unless strictly production and explicitly indexable
  const canIndex = env.isProduction && env.isIndexable;

  if (!canIndex) {
    return {
      robotsMeta: 'noindex, nofollow, noarchive',
      robotsHeader: 'noindex, nofollow, noarchive',
      disallowAll: true
    };
  }

  return {
    robotsMeta: 'index, follow, max-snippet:-1, max-image-preview:large',
    robotsHeader: 'index, follow',
    disallowAll: false
  };
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: Hardcoding indexable meta tags without environment check
export const metadata = {
  robots: 'index, follow' // DEFECT: Staging and preview branches get indexed by Googlebot!
};
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1. Deploy to preview/staging branch.
2. Issue curl request: `curl -sI https://staging.example.com`.
3. Assert presence of `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow`.
4. Inspect `curl -s https://staging.example.com/robots.txt` and assert `Disallow: /`.

## 1190. Automated 50,000-URL Sitemap Chunking & Partitioning Invariant (Harvested from nuxt-modules/sitemap)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [nuxt-modules/sitemap](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/sitemap) (SHA: `306f72108f9d4fe9df9cb6cf3222314b277b5fbd`) and Google Search Central Sitemap Protocol.  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Nuxt sitemap streaming chunker and W3C XML Sitemap schema.

**RULE**:
Any sitemap generation pipeline serving large-scale web applications MUST enforce automated partitioning whenever the total indexed URL count exceeds **50,000 URLs** or uncompressed XML file size exceeds **50 Megabytes (MB)**:
1. **Sitemap Index Parent**: The primary endpoint (`/sitemap.xml` or `/sitemap_index.xml`) MUST serve a `<sitemapindex>` document containing child `<sitemap>` entries.
2. **Chunked Sub-Sitemaps**: Child chunks (`/sitemap-posts-1.xml`, `/sitemap-posts-2.xml`, etc.) MUST each contain at most 45,000 URLs (leaving a safety margin below the 50,000 limit) and provide `<lastmod>` timestamps matching the newest item in that chunk.
3. **Streamed Generation**: Chunks MUST be streamed or generated asynchronously using memory buffers or temporary file streams to prevent Node.js/PHP heap memory exhaustion (`OOM`).
4. **Strict Domain Matching**: All child sitemaps in the index MUST strictly share the exact same scheme, subdomain, and domain as the parent index file.

**WHY**:
Googlebot and search crawlers reject sitemap files exceeding 50,000 URLs or 50MB, generating the fatal Search Console error: *"Sitemap file size limit exceeded: Your Sitemap contains too many URLs. Please create multiple Sitemaps and a Sitemap index file"*. Furthermore, attempting to buffer >100,000 URLs in a single in-memory XML string causes serverless function timeouts and worker node crashes.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- All enterprise sites, e-commerce product catalogs (>10,000 items), news publishers, and dynamic user-generated content directories.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
// Automated Sitemap Chunking & Index Generator
interface SitemapUrl {
  loc: string;
  lastmod: string;
}

export function chunkSitemapUrls(urls: SitemapUrl[], chunkSize = 45000): SitemapUrl[][] {
  const chunks: SitemapUrl[][] = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < urls.length; i += chunkSize) {
    chunks.push(urls.slice(i, i + chunkSize));
  }
  return chunks;
}

export function generateSitemapIndexXml(chunkUrls: { loc: string; lastmod: string }[]): string {
  return [
    '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>',
    '<sitemapindex xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">',
    ...chunkUrls.map(c => `  <sitemap>\n    <loc>${c.loc}</loc>\n    <lastmod>${c.lastmod}</lastmod>\n  </sitemap>`),
    '</sitemapindex>'
  ].join('\n');
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```xml
<!-- ANTI-PATTERN: Emitting single monolithic sitemap with 75,000 URLs -->
<!-- DEFECT: Causes Google Search Console to drop all URLs beyond 50,000 and report fatal error -->
<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">
  <!-- 75,000 <url> tags in one file -->
</urlset>
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1. Run automated linter on output sitemap: assert each chunk XML has `count(//url) <= 50000`.
2. Assert file byte size `< 52428800` bytes (50MB).

## 1191. Server-Side Pre-Rendered OpenGraph Rasterization & Edge Caching Invariant (Harvested from nuxt-modules/og-image)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [nuxt-modules/og-image](https://github.com/nuxt-modules/og-image) (SHA: `ea7dad1284721e42c615e2780152adaf51a34a75`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Satori + resvg rasterization pipeline and Nitro content-hash caching layer.

**RULE**:
Dynamic social media card preview images (OpenGraph / Twitter summary large image) generated from HTML/Vue/React templates MUST:
1. **Lightweight Rasterization**: Be rendered via lightweight JSX/SVG compilation (such as Satori) and rasterized using WebAssembly or native libraries (`resvg`) instead of heavy headless browser instances (Puppeteer/Playwright) in request-handling paths.
2. **Immutable Content-Hash Caching**: Be cached at the server/edge storage tier using a cryptographic hash of component props, template version, and typography assets.
3. **Standard Dimensions**: Explicitly specify `og:image:width` as `1200` and `og:image:height` as `630` in HTML head to prevent social platforms (LinkedIn, Twitter, Facebook, Slack) from degrading or cropping preview cards.

**WHY**:
When a URL is posted to Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, Discord, or WhatsApp, their crawler bots immediately hammer the URL's `og:image` endpoint simultaneously. If dynamic images are rendered using headless Chrome (Puppeteer) on every request, server CPU surges to 100%, lambda memory limits (250MB) are breached, and responses timeout (>10s), causing social platforms to drop the preview card entirely. Pure-wasm Satori + resvg rasterizes in <50ms with <30MB RAM.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- Every dynamic content system generating programmatic social media preview images for blog posts, products, docs, and landing pages.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```html
<head>
  <!-- Verified OpenGraph Social Preview Head Tags -->
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/api/og/post-101.png?v=3a8f9c">
  <meta property="og:image:type" content="image/png">
  <meta property="og:image:width" content="1200">
  <meta property="og:image:height" content="630">
  <meta property="og:image:alt" content="Deep Technical SEO Architecture Visual Guide">
  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
  <meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/api/og/post-101.png?v=3a8f9c">
</head>
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```html
<!-- ANTI-PATTERN: Missing width/height or serving uncompressed 4MB JPEG -->
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/image.jpg">
<!-- Twitter and LinkedIn fall back to small thumbnail or fail to render due to size/ratio -->
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1. Run automated crawler simulation: curl `og:image` URL 10 times in parallel.
2. Assert response time for subsequent hits is `< 25ms` (edge cached).
3. Verify image dimensions are strictly 1200x630.

## 1192. Hydration Mismatch Defense & Zero-JS Static Head Serialization Invariant (Harvested from withastro/astro, nuxt/nuxt, gatsbyjs/gatsby)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [withastro/astro](https://github.com/withastro/astro) (SHA: `484822fb`), [nuxt/nuxt](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt) (SHA: `58124741`), and [gatsbyjs/gatsby](https://github.com/gatsbyjs/gatsby) (SHA: `516700a1`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Unhead SSR serialization, Astro Islands server rendering, and Gatsby Head API.

**RULE**:
All critical search engine metadata—including `<title>`, `<meta name="robots">`, `<link rel="canonical">`, `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="...">`, and JSON-LD structured data—MUST be rendered completely and deterministically into the initial server-side HTML response string before byte delivery. Furthermore:
1. **Zero-JS Static Precedence**: The server HTML stream must be 100% crawlable without executing any client-side JavaScript (as pioneered in Astro Islands architecture).
2. **Deterministic Hydration Keys**: When client JavaScript mounts (e.g. React/Vue hydration), the hydration algorithm MUST NOT destroy, rebuild, or reorder head elements. Every server-rendered tag must carry a deterministic deduplication key or hydration ID.
3. **Zero Content Flapping**: Client code must never emit a differing title or canonical tag than what was served in the initial server HTML, eliminating search engine crawler DOM reconciliation conflicts.

**WHY**:
Search engine crawlers (Googlebot, Bingbot) utilize two-phase crawling. The initial crawl ingests raw server HTML immediately. If the server HTML contains a generic fallback (e.g. `<title>App</title>`) and relies on client-side React/Vue `useEffect()` or `onMounted()` to set the real title, Googlebot's second-stage rendering queue (which may be delayed by hours or days depending on crawl budget) will initially index the blank fallback title. Furthermore, hydration mismatches in HTML head can cause browsers to discard DOM head nodes, triggering duplicate tag injection and premature head closure.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- All SSR, SSG, and hybrid full-stack applications built on Nuxt, Next.js, Astro, Gatsby, SvelteKit, or VuePress.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
// Full-Stack Server-Side Pre-Rendered Head Serialization
export function renderFullHtmlPage(route: { title: string; description: string; canonicalUrl: string; locale: string; schemaJson: string; bodyHtml: string }): string {
  const headElements = [
    '<title>' + route.title + '</title>',
    '<meta name="description" content="' + route.description + '">',
    '<link rel="canonical" href="' + route.canonicalUrl + '">',
    '<script type="application/ld+json">' + route.schemaJson + '</script>'
  ].join('\n  ');

  return '<!DOCTYPE html>\n<html lang="' + route.locale + '">\n<head>\n  <meta charset="utf-8">\n  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">\n  ' + headElements + '\n</head>\n<body>\n  <div id="app">' + route.bodyHtml + '</div>\n</body>\n</html>';
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```javascript
// ANTI-PATTERN: Client-only head mutation in useEffect
function MyPage() {
  useEffect(() => {
    // DEFECT: Raw crawler sees empty title on first byte!
    document.title = "Real SEO Title";
  }, []);
  return <div>Content</div>;
}
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1. Disable JavaScript in curl/browser: `curl -s https://example.com/article | grep -E "<title>|<link rel=\"canonical\"|application/ld\+json"`.
2. Assert that all SEO tags and JSON-LD markup exist in the raw response without any JavaScript execution.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-GGUF) (Revision: `hf-ukisai-`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Any repository distributing non-executable binary artifacts (models, firmware, compiled binaries) MUST include a cryptographic hash manifest (SHA256/SHA512) and a structured metadata manifest (JSON) that explicitly links each binary file to its source version, quantization parameters, and evaluation metrics. The hash manifest MUST be version-controlled alongside the binaries.

**WHY**:
Binary files are opaque. Without a hash manifest, users cannot verify if the file they downloaded matches the intended artifact (preventing supply chain attacks or silent corruption). Without a metadata manifest, users cannot determine if the binary is compatible with their runtime (e.g., MTP support) or if it meets their quality threshold (KLD score). This prevents "silent failures" where a model loads but produces garbage due to version mismatch or corruption.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any Hugging Face, GitHub, or internal artifact repository distributing `.gguf`, `.bin`, `.onnx`, `.wasm`, or firmware images.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```json
// release-manifest.json
{
  "version": "1.5.0",
  "base_model": "ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b",
  "quantization_method": "GSQ-RCO",
  "artifacts": [
    {
      "filename": "Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-IQ2_XS.gguf",
      "sha256": "a1b2c3d4...",
      "size_bytes": 9040000000,
      "quantization_type": "IQ2_XS",
      "kld_dev": 0.189979,
      "features": ["standard"],
      "runtime_requirements": ["llama.cpp >= b4000"]
    },
    {
      "filename": "Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GSQ-RCO-IQ2_XS-mtp.gguf",
      "sha256": "e5f6g7h8...",
      "size_bytes": 9400000000,
      "quantization_type": "IQ2_XS",
      "kld_dev": 0.189979,
      "features": ["standard", "mtp_head"],
      "runtime_requirements": ["llama.cpp >= b4500", "mtp_support"]
    }
  ]
}
```

```markdown

Download the model here: [link]
It works with llama.cpp.
```
*Why it fails:* No hash verification, no version pinning, no feature flags, no quality metrics. User cannot verify integrity or compatibility.

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:

## 1194. Core Web Vitals 75th Percentile Field Invariant (Harvested from GoogleChrome/web-vitals & GoogleChrome/CrUX)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [GoogleChrome/web-vitals](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/web-vitals) (SHA: `d90bf530`) and [GoogleChrome/CrUX](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/CrUX) (SHA: `b62877a0`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Chrome User Experience Report BigQuery schemas and Google Search Page Experience ranking systems.

**RULE**:
All production web systems MUST evaluate and optimize performance against real-user **75th percentile (p75)** field telemetry across a rolling 28-day window, rather than relying exclusively on synthetic lab tests (Lighthouse):
1. **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)**: p75 MUST be `<= 2.5 seconds` on mobile 4G networks.
2. **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)**: p75 MUST be `<= 0.1` across the entire session lifecycle.
3. **INP (Interaction to Next Paint)**: p75 MUST be `<= 200 milliseconds` for all user clicks, taps, and keypresses.
4. **TTFB (Time to First Byte)**: p75 MUST be `<= 800 milliseconds` from initial DNS lookup to first response byte.

CRITICAL INVARIANT: Google Search ranking algorithms evaluate real-user field data aggregated in the Chrome UX Report (CrUX). A site scoring 100/100 in synthetic desktop Lighthouse audits WILL STILL BE PENALIZED if its real mobile users at the 75th percentile experience high CLS or INP failures.

**WHY**:
Synthetic lab audits run under simulated, idealized conditions (fast CPU, clean cache, zero user interactions). Real users visit web applications on mid-to-low tier mobile hardware, with background processes, throttled cellular networks, and long-session interactions. INP measures interaction latency throughout the full user session, meaning a slow JavaScript event handler executed 5 minutes after page load will degrade search ranking signals even if initial page load was fast.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- Every production web property, e-commerce storefront, content publishing network, and web application evaluated by search engine ranking algorithms.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
// Production Field Web Vitals Real-User Monitoring (RUM)
import { onLCP, onCLS, onINP, onTTFB, type Metric } from 'web-vitals';

function sendToAnalytics(metric: Metric): void {
  const body = JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name,
    value: metric.value,
    rating: metric.rating, // 'good' | 'needs-improvement' | 'poor'
    delta: metric.delta,
    id: metric.id,
    navigationType: metric.navigationType
  });

  if (navigator.sendBeacon) {
    navigator.sendBeacon('/api/rum/vitals', body);
  } else {
    fetch('/api/rum/vitals', { body, method: 'POST', keepalive: true });
```

## 1195. Robots Exclusion Longest-Match & 500KB Parser Boundary Invariant (Harvested from google/robotstxt)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [google/robotstxt](https://github.com/google/robotstxt) (SHA: `7d4834ff`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Google's official C++ robots parser implementation adhering to RFC 9309 (Robots Exclusion Protocol).

**RULE**:
All crawler routing systems and SEO validation pipelines MUST strictly conform to RFC 9309 parsing standards:
1. **500KB File Size Limit**: Search engine parsers (including Googlebot) discard all lines in `robots.txt` past byte `512,000` (500 KiB). Placing critical `Disallow:` rules at the end of bloated files results in silent crawl permission.
2. **Precedence via Longest Match**: When conflicting `Allow:` and `Disallow:` rules match a path, the rule with the **longest match pattern** wins. If lengths are identical, the least restrictive rule (`Allow`) takes precedence.
3. **Wildcard Resolution**: Asterisk (`*`) matches 0 or more characters; dollar sign (`$`) asserts end-of-path. Query parameters not explicitly terminated with `$` match prefix URLs.

**WHY**:
Webmasters frequently concatenate third-party disallow lists, security rules, and user-agent blocks into massive `robots.txt` files. If the file exceeds 500KB, crawlers truncate parsing, silently exposing staging environments, admin endpoints, or infinite crawl traps. Furthermore, developers assume line order dictates precedence (like firewall rules); RFC 9309 explicitly mandates longest-match resolution regardless of line position.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- Dynamic `robots.txt` generation endpoints, automated SEO audits, proxy crawlers, and staging isolation configurations.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
export function validateRobotsTxtBuffer(buffer: Buffer): { isValid: boolean; byteLength: number; errors: string[] } {
  const MAX_ROBOTS_BYTES = 512 * 1024; // 500 KiB RFC 9309 limit
  const byteLength = buffer.byteLength;
  const errors: string[] = [];

  if (byteLength > MAX_ROBOTS_BYTES) {
    errors.push(
      `Robots.txt size (${byteLength} bytes) exceeds RFC 9309 limit (${MAX_ROBOTS_BYTES} bytes). Directives beyond this point will be ignored by Googlebot.`
    );
  }

  return {
    isValid: errors.length === 0,
    byteLength,
    errors
  };
}
```

## 1196. Dynamic Rendering Soft-404 Elimination Invariant (Harvested from prerender/prerender)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [prerender/prerender](https://github.com/prerender/prerender) (SHA: `3b32eec0`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Prerender.io middleware and Google Search Console indexing error tracking.

**RULE**:
Dynamic rendering proxies and Single-Page Application (SPA) pre-render pipelines MUST NEVER return an HTTP `200 OK` status header when the rendered client-side route represents a 404/not-found or 500/error condition:
1. **Status Code Meta Tag Header Interception**: The headless renderer MUST detect `<meta name="prerender-status-code" content="404">` injected into the rendered DOM and force the upstream proxy response to output exact HTTP status code `404 Not Found`.
2. **Location Header Redirection**: The headless renderer MUST detect `<meta name="prerender-header" content="Location: https://example.com/target">` and issue an immediate HTTP 301/302 response rather than serving rendered HTML.
3. **Soft-404 Zero Tolerance**: Delivering HTTP 200 with DOM content saying "Page Not Found", "Product Unavailable", or empty route state causes search engines to flag "Soft 404" errors, wasting crawl budget and corrupting search indexes.

**WHY**:
Client-side routers (React Router, Vue Router, SvelteKit) render entirely inside the browser. When an invalid route or missing product is requested, client-side JavaScript renders a nice 404 visual component, but the web server that served the initial HTML shell responded with `HTTP 200 OK`. Headless crawlers capturing this HTML report HTTP 200 to Googlebot, causing severe Soft 404 indexing penalties across thousands of URLs.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- Headless rendering clusters, Prerender middleware, SSR fallback handlers, and client-side single-page applications.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```javascript
// Middleware: Express/Node.js Prerender status code extractor
function extractPrerenderStatusCode(html) {
  const match = html.match(/<meta[^>]+name=["']prerender-status-code["'][^>]+content=["'](\d{3})["']/i);
  return match ? parseInt(match[1], 10) : 200;
}

export function handleRenderedResponse(req, res, renderedHtml) {
  const statusCode = extractPrerenderStatusCode(renderedHtml);
  
  if (statusCode === 404) {
    res.status(404).set('Content-Type', 'text/html; charset=utf-8').send(renderedHtml);
    return;
  }
  
  if (statusCode === 301 || statusCode === 302) {
    const locMatch = renderedHtml.match(/<meta[^>]+name=["']prerender-header["'][^>]+content=["']Location:\s*([^"']+)["']/i);
    if (locMatch) {
      res.redirect(statusCode, locMatch[1]);
      return;
    }
  }

  res.status(200).set('Content-Type', 'text/html; charset=utf-8').send(renderedHtml);
}
```

## 1197. Above-the-Fold Critical CSS Inlining & Non-Blocking Async Invariant (Harvested from addyosmani/critical)

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [addyosmani/critical](https://github.com/addyosmani/critical) (SHA: `db6f0c2a`).  
> **Evidence**: Confirmed in Critical CSS generation algorithms, Puppeteer viewport layout extraction, and PageSpeed Insights audits.

**RULE**:
To achieve zero-render-blocking LCP under Core Web Vitals, all production HTML pages MUST inline critical above-the-fold CSS directly into the HTML `<head>` and defer remaining non-critical styles:
1. **Critical CSS Inlining**: Extract and inline CSS rules required to render viewport dimensions `1300x900` (desktop) and `375x667` (mobile) into an inline `<style>` block in `<head>`.
2. **14KB TCP cwnd Budget**: The inlined critical CSS plus initial HTML MUST NOT exceed 14 KiB (uncompressed/first TCP packet window) to prevent extra round trips before First Contentful Paint (FCP).
3. **Non-Blocking Async Deferral**: The full stylesheet bundle MUST be loaded asynchronously using `<link rel="preload" as="style" onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">` accompanied by a `<noscript>` fallback.

**WHY**:
External stylesheets are render-blocking resources. Browsers halt HTML parsing and page rendering until all external CSS files referenced in `<head>` are downloaded, parsed, and applied to the DOM tree. Inlining critical CSS enables instant FCP and LCP within the first round-trip time (RTT), directly driving Google Core Web Vitals into the "Good" range.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
- High-performance marketing sites, e-commerce landing pages, and content blogs requiring sub-second FCP/LCP.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>High Performance Page</title>
  
  <!-- 1. Inline Critical CSS (Below 14KB cwnd budget) -->
  <style>
    body{margin:0;font-family:system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif}
    .hero{display:flex;min-height:60vh;background:#0d1117;color:#fff;padding:2rem}
    .hero h1{font-size:2.5rem;line-height:1.2}
  </style>

  <!-- 2. Asynchronous Non-Blocking Full Stylesheet Load -->
  <link rel="preload" href="/css/main.bundle.css" as="style" onload="this.onload=null;this.rel='stylesheet'">
  <noscript><link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/main.bundle.css"></noscript>
</head>
<body>
  <div class="hero">
    <h1>Sub-Second Largest Contentful Paint</h1>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
```

**RULE**:
When deploying LLMs on consumer hardware, **MUST** validate that quantization (e.g., 4-bit, 8-bit) does not degrade critical benchmark scores (e.g., ARC-C, MMLU) below acceptable thresholds. **MUST NOT** assume that lower bit-width always results in proportional performance loss without empirical benchmarking.

**WHY**:
Quantization introduces rounding errors in weight matrices. While 4-bit quantization reduces memory footprint by 4x, it can lead to significant accuracy drops in complex reasoning tasks. The README claims 4-bit achieves 719 ARC-C, which is close to the 8-bit score (735), suggesting careful quantization (e.g., using imatrix) mitigates this loss. Without validation, users may deploy models that fail in production reasoning tasks.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any LLM deployment pipeline involving quantization (GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ) for edge or consumer hardware.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Pseudocode for quantization validation
def validate_quantization(base_model, quantized_model, benchmark_suite):
    base_score = benchmark_suite.evaluate(base_model)
    quant_score = benchmark_suite.evaluate(quantized_model)
    
    # Define acceptable degradation threshold (e.g., 5% relative drop)
    threshold = 0.05
    relative_drop = (base_score - quant_score) / base_score
    
    if relative_drop > threshold:
        raise ValueError(f"Quantization degraded performance by {relative_drop*100}%. "
                         f"Base: {base_score}, Quant: {quant_score}")
    
    return quant_score

# Usage

```


```python
def evaluate_thinking_efficiency(model, prompt, max_thinking_tokens):
```

**RULE**:
When fine-tuning LLMs for specialized capabilities (e.g., coding, creative writing), **MUST** use multi-stage fine-tuning to ensure that the model retains general capabilities while acquiring specialized skills. **MUST NOT** fine-tune on a single dataset without validating that general capabilities are not degraded.

**WHY**:
Single-stage fine-tuning can lead to "catastrophic forgetting," where the model loses general knowledge while acquiring specialized skills. The README mentions "multi-stage tuned" and "multi-state-merge," suggesting that the model was fine-tuned in multiple stages to balance specialized and general capabilities. Without this, the model may be excellent at coding but poor at general conversation.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Fine-tuning LLMs for specialized domains (e.g., coding, medical, legal) while maintaining general conversational abilities.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Pseudocode for multi-stage fine-tuning validation
def validate_multi_stage_finetuning(base_model, stage1_model, stage2_model, general_benchmark, specialized_benchmark):
    base_general = general_benchmark.evaluate(base_model)
    stage1_general = general_benchmark.evaluate(stage1_model)
    stage2_general = general_benchmark.evaluate(stage2_model)
    
    base_specialized = specialized_benchmark.evaluate(base_model)
    stage1_specialized = specialized_benchmark.evaluate(stage1_model)
    stage2_specialized = specialized_benchmark.evaluate(stage2_model)
    
    # Ensure general capabilities are not significantly degraded
    if stage2_general < base_general * 0.9:
        raise ValueError("General capabilities degraded by more than 10%")
    
    # Ensure specialized capabilities are improved
    if stage2_specialized < base_specialized:
        raise ValueError("Specialized capabilities not improved")
    
    return {
        "general_score": stage2_general,
        "specialized_score": stage2_specialized
    }

# Usage
```

**RULE**:  
All special token IDs (`bos_token_id`, `eos_token_id`, `pad_token_id`, `image_token_id`, `audio_token_id`, etc.) defined in `config.json` and `tokenizer_config.json` **must be identical** across the tokenizer, the model configuration, and the inference pipeline.

**WHY**:  
Mismatched token IDs cause the model to misinterpret padding, start/end markers, or multimodal tokens, leading to corrupted hidden states, incorrect attention masks, and ultimately invalid logits or runtime errors (e.g., `IndexError` when accessing out‑of‑range token embeddings).

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
During model packaging, tokenizer creation, and inference pipeline construction for any HuggingFace‑based multimodal model that relies on explicit token ID mapping.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# config.json
{
  "bos_token_id": 248044,
  "eos_token_id": 248044,
  "pad_token_id": 248044,
  "image_token_id": 248056,
  "audio_token_id": 248058
}

# tokenizer_config.json
{
  "bos_token_id": 248044,
  "eos_token_id": 248044,
  "pad_token_id": 248044,
  "image_token_id": 248056,
  "audio_token_id": 248058
}

# inference pipeline
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(path)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(path)

assert tokenizer.bos_token_id == model.config.bos_token_id
assert tokenizer.eos_token_id == model.config.eos_token_id
assert tokenizer.pad_token_id == model.config.pad_token_id
assert tokenizer.image_token_id == model.config.image_token_id
assert tokenizer.audio_token_id == model.config.audio_token_id
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

# tokenizer.bos_token_id != model.config.bos_token_id → runtime failure
```

**RULE**:  
The hidden size of the joint schema head **must equal** the hidden size of the backbone’s final hidden state (`model.config.hidden_size`).

**WHY**:  
The joint head receives the backbone’s final hidden states as input. A mismatch in dimensionality leads to a `RuntimeError` during matrix multiplication or silent broadcasting errors that corrupt logits.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
When defining a new joint head or modifying the backbone architecture.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:

```python
  "num_attention_heads": 24,
  "num_hidden_layers": 64
}
```

**RULE**:  
> **MUST** guarantee that the joint head’s output tensor has shape `(batch_size, total_options)` where `total_options` equals the sum of `len(question.option_ids)` for all questions in the batch.

**WHY**:  
If the output shape is incorrect, downstream softmax will produce NaNs or mis‑aligned probabilities, breaking the decision logic.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
During the forward pass of the joint head and when constructing the `question_masks` tensor.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**  
```python
class JointHead(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, hidden_states, question_masks):
        logits = self.transformer(hidden_states)  # (B, T, H)
        # Project to per‑question logits
        logits = self.proj(logits)  # (B, T, Q)
        # Flatten per‑question logits
        logits = logits.view(logits.size(0), -1)  # (B, total_options)
        # Apply masks to zero out padding options
        logits = logits * question_masks
        return logits
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**  
```python
# BAD: Using a fixed output size regardless of question count
logits = self.proj(hidden_states)  # (B, T, 10)  # hard‑coded 10 options
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**  
* Property test that feeds a batch with varying numbers of questions and asserts `logits.shape[1] == sum(len(q.option_ids) for q in batch)`.

**RULE**:  
> **MUST** ensure that `encode_record()` is deterministic: the same input record must always produce identical token ids and image tensors, regardless of the order of keys in the JSON.

**WHY**:  
Non‑deterministic encoding leads to inconsistent batching and unpredictable logits, making unit tests flaky and production inference unreliable.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:  
During the implementation of `encode_record()` and any helper that serialises the record.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**  
```python
def encode_record(tokenizer, record, processor):
    # 1. Canonicalise JSON order
    state_str = json.dumps(record["state"], sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    # 2. Tokenise state
    state_ids = tokenizer.encode(state_str, add_special_tokens=False)
    # 3. Process images/videos
    image_tensors = []
    for img in record.get("images", []):
        image_tensors.append(processor.process_image(img))
    # 4. Concatenate
    return {
        "input_ids": torch.tensor(state_ids, dtype=torch.long),
        "image_tensors": torch.stack(image_tensors) if image_tensors else None,
        "questions": record["questions"],
    }
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**  
```python

```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**  
* Unit test that serialises the same record twice and asserts equality of the resulting tensors.

**RULE**:
When deploying a pretrained NLP model, the tokenizer configuration (specifically `do_lower_case`, `padding_side`, and `truncation_strategy`) MUST be byte-for-byte identical to the configuration used during pretraining. Any deviation in preprocessing invalidates the learned embeddings.

**WHY**:
BERT's embeddings are learned based on specific token distributions. If `do_lower_case` is `True` during pretraining but `False` during inference, the token IDs for "English" and "english" will differ. The model will treat them as distinct, unseen tokens (or map them to different vectors), causing a catastrophic drop in accuracy (often >20% F1 drop on classification tasks). This is a silent failure mode; the model runs without error but produces garbage outputs.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system loading a Hugging Face `PreTrainedModel` or `AutoTokenizer`. Applies to Python, JavaScript (transformers.js), and C++ (ONNX Runtime) implementations.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python

# 1. Load tokenizer with EXACT config from repo
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google-bert/bert-base-uncased")

# 2. Verify invariant at runtime (Forensic Check)
assert tokenizer.do_lower_case == True, "Tokenizer config mismatch: do_lower_case must be True"
assert tokenizer.model_max_length == 512, "Max length mismatch"

# 3. Inference
inputs = tokenizer("Hello World", return_tensors="pt")
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("google-bert/bert-base-uncased")
outputs = model(**inputs)
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:

```python
def verify_tokenizer_invariant(repo_id: str):

    config = requests.get(url).json()
```

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [google-bert/bert-base-uncased](https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-uncased) (Revision: `hf-google-`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When serializing or transferring model weights between frameworks (PyTorch to ONNX, FP32 to FP16), the `layer_norm_eps` (epsilon) MUST be preserved or explicitly adjusted to match the target precision's machine epsilon. Using a fixed epsilon of $10^{-12}$ in FP16 (half-precision) leads to division by zero or NaN propagation.

**WHY**:
Layer Normalization computes $\frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}$. In FP32, $10^{-12}$ is safe. In FP16, the smallest positive normal number is $\approx 6 \times 10^{-5}$, and subnormals go down to $\approx 6 \times 10^{-8}$. An epsilon of $10^{-12}$ underflows to 0 in FP16. If $\sigma^2$ is also very small, the denominator becomes 0, causing `inf` or `nan` in the output, which propagates through the network.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Quantization pipelines, ONNX export, TensorRT optimization, or any mixed-precision training/inference.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch

# FP32: Standard epsilon
config_fp32 = {"layer_norm_eps": 1e-12}

# FP16: Adjusted epsilon to avoid underflow
# Machine epsilon for float16 is approx 1e-3, but safe floor is often 1e-5 or 1e-6
config_fp16 = {"layer_norm_eps": 1e-5} 

def export_to_onnx(model, config):
    # Dynamically set epsilon based on dtype
    if model.dtype == torch.float16:
        config["layer_norm_eps"] = 1e-5
    else:
        config["layer_norm_eps"] = 1e-12
    # ... export logic
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: Blindly using FP32 epsilon in FP16 pipeline
model.half() # Convert to FP16
# config.json still has layer_norm_eps: 1e-12
# Result: NaNs in LayerNorm outputs
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
```python
import torch

def check_epsilon_safety(dtype, epsilon):
    if dtype == torch.float16:
        min_positive = torch.finfo(torch.float16).tiny
        if epsilon < min_positive:
            return False, f"Epsilon {epsilon} underflows in FP16 (min: {min_positive})"
    return True, "Safe"
```

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [google-bert/bert-base-uncased](https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-uncased) (Revision: `hf-google-`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When input text exceeds `max_position_embeddings` (512 for BERT-base), the truncation strategy MUST be explicitly defined (left, right, or middle) and consistent with the downstream task's semantic requirements. Default truncation (usually right) silently discards information.

**WHY**:
BERT uses absolute position embeddings. It cannot handle sequences longer than 512 tokens. If a document is 1000 tokens, the last 488 tokens are ignored. For tasks like "Summarize the end of the document," right-truncation destroys the signal. For "Classify the beginning," left-truncation is wrong. Silent truncation leads to "hallucinated" confidence scores on missing data.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any NLP pipeline processing variable-length documents.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
def safe_tokenize(text, tokenizer, max_len=512, strategy="left"):
    # 1. Check length
    tokens = tokenizer(text, truncation=False)
    if len(tokens["input_ids"]) <= max_len:
        return tokens
    
    # 2. Apply explicit strategy
    if strategy == "left":
        # Keep last max_len tokens
        tokens = tokenizer(text, truncation=True, truncation_side="right", max_length=max_len)
    elif strategy == "right":
        # Keep first max_len tokens
        tokens = tokenizer(text, truncation=True, truncation_side="left", max_length=max_len)
    else:
        raise ValueError("Invalid truncation strategy")
        
    return tokens
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: Assuming tokenizer handles long text gracefully
inputs = tokenizer(long_text, return_tensors="pt") 
# If long_text > 512, this raises an error or silently truncates depending on version.
# No explicit strategy = unpredictable behavior.
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
```python
def test_truncation_invariant():
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
    long_text = "word " * 1000
    
    # Test right truncation
    t1 = tokenizer(long_text, truncation=True, truncation_side="right", max_length=512)
    assert len(t1["input_ids"]) == 512
    # Verify it kept the END of the text
    assert t1["input_ids"][-1] != tokenizer("word")["input_ids"][0] # Last token should be from end
    
    # Test left truncation
    t2 = tokenizer(long_text, truncation=True, truncation_side="left", max_length=512)
    assert len(t2["input_ids"]) == 512
    # Verify it kept the START of the text
    assert t2["input_ids"][0] == tokenizer("word")["input_ids"][0]
```

**RULE**:
Any neural network model that expects normalized inputs MUST NOT accept raw pixel values (0-255) directly. The inference pipeline MUST enforce a strict preprocessing step that applies the exact mean and standard deviation defined in the model's `pretrained_cfg` before tensor conversion.
**WHY**:
Neural networks are trained on normalized distributions. Feeding raw pixels (range 0-255) instead of normalized values (range ~-2 to +2) causes the input to fall far outside the training distribution. This leads to **silent failure**: the model runs without error but produces garbage probabilities (e.g., all zeros or uniform distribution). This is a "silent data corruption" bug that is extremely difficult to debug because no exception is thrown.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
All PyTorch/TensorFlow inference pipelines, especially when integrating third-party models from Hugging Face or timm.
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
from PIL import Image
import timm

def safe_inference(model, image_path):
    # 1. Resolve config from model, do NOT hardcode
    data_config = timm.data.resolve_model_data_config(model)
    
    # 2. Create transform using resolved config
    # is_training=False ensures no random augmentation
    transforms = timm.data.create_transform(**data_config, is_training=False)
    
    # 3. Load and transform
    img = Image.open(image_path)
    tensor = transforms(img).unsqueeze(0) # Add batch dimension
    
    # 4. Inference
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model(tensor)
        
    return output
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

def unsafe_inference(model, image_path):
    img = Image.open(image_path)
    tensor = torch.from_numpy(np.array(img)).float() / 255.0 # WRONG: Does not apply mean/std
    tensor = tensor.unsqueeze(0).permute(0, 3, 1, 2)
    # This will produce incorrect results for models expecting ImageNet normalization
    return model(tensor)
```

```python
        final_feature = features[-1]
    else:
        final_feature = features
```

Distillation compresses the trajectory of the diffusion process. If the inference scheduler attempts to use 20+ steps on a model trained for 4 steps, the model's learned velocity field becomes invalid, leading to artifacting, color shifts, or complete failure to converge. The "fast" variant is only fast and accurate within its specific step budget.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:

> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Any inference engine serving a Transformer-based LLM MUST enforce a hard limit on the total number of tokens in the KV cache (Key-Value cache) per request and globally, based on available GPU memory. The system MUST NOT allow unbounded sequence growth that exceeds the pre-allocated KV cache buffer.

**WHY**:
The KV cache grows linearly with sequence length. If not bounded, a single long-running request or a burst of concurrent requests will exhaust GPU memory, causing Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crashes or silent data corruption if the allocator fails gracefully. In Llama-3-8B, the KV cache size is a significant fraction of total memory (especially with GQA).

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system implementing autoregressive generation for Transformer models (vLLM, TGI, custom CUDA kernels).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
class KVCacheManager:
    def __init__(self, max_batch_size, max_seq_len, num_layers, num_kv_heads, head_dim, dtype):
        # Pre-allocate contiguous memory for KV cache
        self.k_cache = torch.empty(
            (max_batch_size, max_seq_len, num_layers, num_kv_heads, head_dim),
            dtype=dtype, device='cuda'
        )
        self.v_cache = torch.empty_like(self.k_cache)
        self.max_seq_len = max_seq_len
        self.current_lengths = torch.zeros(max_batch_size, dtype=torch.int32, device='cuda')

    def append(self, batch_idx, k, v):
        current_len = self.current_lengths[batch_idx].item()
        if current_len >= self.max_seq_len:
            raise MemoryError("KV Cache full. Sequence length exceeded limit.")
        
        # Write to pre-allocated buffer
        self.k_cache[batch_idx, current_len] = k
        self.v_cache[batch_idx, current_len] = v
        self.current_lengths[batch_idx] += 1

    def reset(self, batch_idx):
        self.current_lengths[batch_idx] = 0
        # Optional: Zero out memory for security (prevent data leakage between requests)
        self.k_cache[batch_idx].zero_()
        self.v_cache[batch_idx].zero_()
```

```python

class BadKVCache:
    def __init__(self):
        self.k_cache = []  # Unbounded list

    def append(self, k):
        self.k_cache.append(k)  # Will cause OOM if sequence is long
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Unit Test**: Simulate a sequence of length `max_seq_len + 1`. Assert that `MemoryError` is raised at the `max_seq_len + 1`-th token.
2.  **Memory Profiling**: Use `nvidia-smi` or `torch.cuda.memory_allocated()` to verify that memory usage plateaus at the pre-allocated size and does not grow with sequence length.

**RULE**:
Any system formatting prompts for an instruction-tuned LLM (like Llama-3-8B) MUST strictly adhere to the model's defined chat template, including the correct placement of special tokens (`<|begin_of_text|>`, `<|start_header_id|>`, etc.). The system MUST NOT allow user input to inject or override these special tokens.

**WHY**:
Llama-3-8B is fine-tuned on a specific chat format. Deviating from this format (e.g., missing `<|eot_id|>` or incorrect role headers) leads to severe performance degradation, hallucinations, or the model ignoring instructions. Furthermore, if user input can inject special tokens, it can break the model's parsing logic or lead to prompt injection attacks.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any frontend or API layer that constructs prompts for Llama-3-8B-Instruct.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import re

def format_prompt(system, user, assistant_history):
    # Define the exact template for Llama-3-8B
    template = "<|begin_of_text|>{% for message in messages %}{% if message['role'] == 'system' %}<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>\n\n{{ message['content'] }}<|eot_id|>{% elif message['role'] == 'user' %}<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>\n\n{{ message['content'] }}<|eot_id|>{% elif message['role'] == 'assistant' %}<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>\n\n{{ message['content'] }}<|eot_id|>{% endif %}{% endfor %}"
    
    messages = []
    if system:
        messages.append({"role": "system", "content": system})
    for msg in assistant_history:
        messages.append(msg)
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": user})
    
    # Sanitize user input to prevent special token injection
    sanitized_user = re.sub(r'<\|.*?\|>', '', user)
    messages[-1]["content"] = sanitized_user
    
    # Use a Jinja2-like renderer or manual string replacement
    # For simplicity, manual construction:
    prompt = "<|begin_of_text|>"
    for msg in messages:
        prompt += f"<|start_header_id|>{msg['role']}<|end_header_id|>\n\n{msg['content']}<|eot_id|>"
    
    return prompt
```

```python
    for i in range(config['num_hidden_layers']):
```

**RULE**:
In any autoregressive transformer inference system, the Key-Value (KV) cache MUST be explicitly bounded by a maximum sequence length (`max_seq_len`) and MUST implement a sliding window or eviction strategy if the context exceeds the model's trained positional encoding limit. The system MUST NOT allow unbounded memory growth proportional to input length without a hard cap.

**WHY**:
The KV cache stores attention keys and values for all previous tokens. For a 7B model with 32 layers and 4096 hidden dim, each token adds ~128KB of memory (FP16). Without a cap, a 100k-token context will consume ~12.8GB *just for cache*, leading to OOM (Out of Memory) crashes or GPU memory fragmentation. Unbounded growth violates the finite resource constraint of GPU VRAM.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any LLM inference server, local inference client, or fine-tuning loop that uses autoregressive generation.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
class BoundedKVCache:
    def __init__(self, max_seq_len: int, num_layers: int, num_heads: int, head_dim: int, dtype=torch.float16):
        self.max_seq_len = max_seq_len
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.head_dim = head_dim
        self.dtype = dtype
        # Pre-allocate max possible cache to avoid dynamic resizing
        self.k_cache = torch.zeros(num_layers, num_heads, max_seq_len, head_dim, dtype=dtype)
        self.v_cache = torch.zeros(num_layers, num_heads, max_seq_len, head_dim, dtype=dtype)
        self.current_len = 0

    def update(self, layer_idx: int, k_new: torch.Tensor, v_new: torch.Tensor):
        if self.current_len >= self.max_seq_len:
            # Shift cache left by 1 (sliding window) or raise error
            self.k_cache[layer_idx] = self.k_cache[layer_idx, 1:].clone()
            self.v_cache[layer_idx] = self.v_cache[layer_idx, 1:].clone()
            self.k_cache[layer_idx, 0] = k_new
            self.v_cache[layer_idx, 0] = v_new
        else:
            self.k_cache[layer_idx, self.current_len] = k_new
            self.v_cache[layer_idx, self.current_len] = v_new
            self.current_len += 1

    def get(self, layer_idx: int):
        return self.k_cache[layer_idx, :self.current_len], self.v_cache[layer_idx, :self.current_len]
```

```python
        self.v_cache.append(v_new)
```

Silent truncation loses critical context; ignoring bounds leads to garbage outputs.

**RULE**:
The tokenizer MUST guarantee that `detokenize(tokenize(text)) == text` for all valid inputs, or MUST explicitly document and handle cases where round-trip fidelity is lost (e.g., special tokens, whitespace normalization). The system MUST NOT assume that token IDs map 1:1 to characters.

**WHY**:
BPE tokenizers split text into subwords. Whitespace handling, special tokens (e.g., `<s>`, `</s>`), and Unicode normalization can cause discrepancies. If the system assumes round-trip fidelity, it will corrupt data in pipelines that rely on exact string matching (e.g., RAG retrieval, code generation).

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system that uses a tokenizer for data preprocessing, RAG, or code generation.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
def safe_detokenize(tokenizer, token_ids):
    # Use tokenizer's built-in method which handles special tokens
    text = tokenizer.decode(token_ids, skip_special_tokens=False)
    # Post-process if needed (e.g., remove leading/trailing whitespace)
    return text.strip()

def verify_round_trip(tokenizer, text):
    tokens = tokenizer.encode(text)
    decoded = safe_detokenize(tokenizer, tokens)
    if decoded != text:
        # Log warning or handle discrepancy
        print(f"Warning: Round-trip mismatch. Original: {text}, Decoded: {decoded}")
    return decoded
```


**RULE**:
When deploying a LoRA or adapter for a specific task (e.g., camera control, style transfer), the **inference prompt** MUST semantically align with the **training objective** of the adapter. The prompt must explicitly constrain the degrees of freedom that the adapter is *not* responsible for (e.g., if the LoRA controls camera, the prompt must freeze object motion).

**WHY**:
Generative models rely on cross-attention to bind text tokens to visual features. If the prompt allows ambiguity (e.g., "a man walking"), the base model's prior will conflict with the LoRA's learned trajectory, causing artifacts, jitter, or failure to converge. The LoRA learns a *delta* in the latent space; the prompt defines the *context* in which that delta is applied. Misalignment leads to "fighting" between the base prior and the adapter, resulting in degraded quality or hallucination.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
*   Any system using LoRA, DreamBooth, or fine-tuned adapters for diffusion models.
*   Specifically in video generation where temporal consistency is required.
*   When combining multiple adapters (e.g., style + motion).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:

```python
prompt = (
    "One frozen instant. Only the camera moves. In a continuous 360 orbit. "
    "Preserve every person and object in exactly the same world position, "
    "orientation, shape and pose throughout the shot. "
    "Airborne objects remain suspended at the captured height and angle: "
    "no wobbling, shaking, spinning, drifting, falling or continued action. "
    "Keep faces, hands, clothing, liquids and the background motionless. "
    "Camera parallax is the only source of apparent movement."
)

# Inference call

    prompt=prompt,
    first_frame=input_image,
    last_frame=input_image,  # Symmetric keyframes for looping
    lora_weights="pablodawson/MiniMax-H3-360-Orbit-LoRA",
```

```python
# Result: The base model may animate the man's hair, clothes, or background,
# breaking the "frozen instant" invariant and causing temporal flickering.
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Visual Regression Test**: Generate 10 samples with the aligned prompt and 10 with a vague prompt.
2.  **Optical Flow Analysis**: Compute the optical flow magnitude for non-camera regions. For the aligned prompt, the flow magnitude in object regions MUST be near zero (< threshold). For the vague prompt, it will be non-zero.
3.  **Loop Seam Check**: Compare Frame 0 and Frame N-1 pixel-wise. The difference MUST be below a perceptual threshold (e.g., SSIM > 0.95) to ensure seamless looping.

**RULE**:
To generate a seamless looping video using First-Last Frame (FL2V) models, the **first frame** and **last frame** inputs MUST be identical (or perceptually identical) images. The model MUST be conditioned on this symmetry to infer a closed-loop trajectory.

**WHY**:

If `First_Frame == Last_Frame`, the model is constrained to a path that starts and ends at A, forcing a circular or orbital trajectory. Without this symmetry, the model will drift, causing a visible "jump" or "seam" when the video is looped in a player.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:

*   FL2V (First-Last Frame to Video) architectures.
*   When stitching multiple video clips together.

```python
    last_frame=last_frame,
```

**RULE**:
The diffusion transformer's output latent tensor dimensions MUST strictly match the VAE decoder's expected input dimensions. Any mismatch in spatial resolution (H, W) or channel count (C) MUST trigger an immediate `ValueError` before the VAE decode step, not a silent broadcast error or shape mismatch crash during tensor operations.

**WHY**:
Diffusion models operate in a compressed latent space. The VAE (Variational Autoencoder) is responsible for mapping latents back to pixel space. If the transformer outputs a latent of shape `[B, C, H, W]` but the VAE expects `[B, C', H', W']`, PyTorch/TensorFlow may attempt implicit broadcasting, leading to:
1.  **Silent Corruption**: If dimensions are compatible via broadcasting (e.g., `1` vs `N`), the output image will be geometrically distorted or contain artifacts.
2.  **Memory Explosion**: If dimensions are incompatible but large, the system may attempt to allocate a massive intermediate tensor, causing OOM (Out of Memory) crashes.
3.  **Debugging Nightmare**: Shape mismatches in deep neural networks are notoriously difficult to trace back to the source if not caught at the boundary.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
*   Any generative AI pipeline involving a VAE (Stable Diffusion, Flux, DALL-E 3, etc.).
*   When implementing custom schedulers or transformers that modify latent shapes.
*   During model loading, when verifying `config.json` parameters against actual weight shapes.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
from typing import Tuple

def validate_latent_shape(latent: torch.Tensor, vae_config: dict) -> None:
    """
    Enforces strict dimensional integrity between transformer output and VAE input.
    """
    expected_channels = vae_config['in_channels']
    # VAEs often expect specific spatial downsampling factors (e.g., 8x)
    # This check ensures the latent is not accidentally upsampled/downsampled incorrectly.
    
    if latent.dim() != 4:
        raise ValueError(f"Latent must be 4D [B, C, H, W], got {latent.dim()}D")
    
    b, c, h, w = latent.shape
    
    if c != expected_channels:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Channel mismatch: Transformer output has {c} channels, "
            f"but VAE expects {expected_channels}. Check model config or transformer head."
        )
    
    # Optional: Check spatial dimensions if the pipeline enforces fixed resolution
    # if h % 8 != 0 or w % 8 != 0:
    #     raise ValueError("Latent spatial dimensions must be divisible by VAE downscale factor (8).")

# Usage in Pipeline
def decode_latents(self, latents: torch.Tensor):
    validate_latent_shape(latents, self.vae.config)
    # Safe to proceed with VAE decode
    image = self.vae.decode(latents / self.vae.config.scaling_factor).sample
    return image
```

**RULE**:
The noise scheduler's initial noise generation MUST be deterministic for a given seed. The seed MUST be applied to the CPU before any GPU operations, and the noise tensor MUST be cast to the same dtype and device as the model weights before being added to the latent.

**WHY**:
1.  **Reproducibility**: Users expect that `seed=42` always produces the same image. If the seed is applied on GPU or after dtype conversion, floating-point non-determinism (due to CUDA kernel variations) will break reproducibility.
2.  **Dtype Mismatch**: If the noise is `float32` and the model is `float16`, adding them will upcast the latent to `float32`, doubling memory usage and potentially causing overflow in subsequent `float16` operations.
3.  **Device Mismatch**: If noise is on CPU and latent is on GPU, the addition will trigger a synchronous device transfer, causing a massive latency spike.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
*   Any diffusion model inference pipeline.
*   When implementing custom schedulers (DDIM, Euler, DPM-Solver).
*   When supporting mixed-precision training/inference.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
import numpy as np

def generate_deterministic_noise(shape: tuple, seed: int, device: torch.device, dtype: torch.dtype) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Generates noise deterministically on CPU, then moves to target device/dtype.
    """
    # 1. Seed on CPU for determinism
    generator = torch.Generator(device='cpu').manual_seed(seed)
    
    # 2. Generate noise on CPU in float32 (standard for RNG)
    noise = torch.randn(shape, generator=generator, device='cpu', dtype=torch.float32)
    
    # 3. Move to target device and dtype
    # This ensures the noise is in the correct format before being added to latents
    noise = noise.to(device=device, dtype=dtype)
    
    return noise

# Usage in Pipeline
def prepare_latents(self, batch_size, num_channels, height, width, dtype, device, generator=None, seed=None):
    if seed is not None:
        noise = generate_deterministic_noise(
            (batch_size, num_channels, height, width), 
            seed, 
            device, 
            dtype
        )
    else:
        noise = torch.randn((batch_size, num_channels, height, width), device=device, dtype=dtype)
    
    # Scale noise according to scheduler
    latents = noise * self.scheduler.init_noise_sigma
    return latents
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

def prepare_latents_bad(self, batch_size, num_channels, height, width, dtype, device, seed=None):
    if seed is not None:
        # BAD: Seeding on GPU is non-deterministic across CUDA versions
        torch.manual_seed(seed) 
        # BAD: Generating directly on GPU may use different RNG kernels
        noise = torch.randn((batch_size, num_channels, height, width), device=device)
        # BAD: If dtype is float16, this noise is float32 by default, causing upcast
    else:
        noise = torch.randn((batch_size, num_channels, height, width), device=device)
    
    latents = noise * self.scheduler.init_noise_sigma
    return latents
```

*   **Integration Test**: Run inference with `seed=42` twice. Assert that the output images are identical (pixel-perfect match).
*   **Dtype Check**: Assert that `noise.dtype == model.dtype` after generation.

**RULE**:
The text tokenizer's output `input_ids` and `attention_mask` MUST be padded to the same length as the maximum sequence length in the batch. The `attention_mask` MUST be `1` for real tokens and `0` for padding. The transformer's attention mechanism MUST use this mask to ignore padding tokens.

**WHY**:
1.  **Attention Leakage**: If the attention mask is not applied, the transformer will attend to padding tokens, which are arbitrary values (usually 0). This introduces noise into the attention weights, degrading image quality.
2.  **Batch Inefficiency**: If sequences are not padded to the same length, the batch cannot be processed in parallel, leading to sequential processing and massive latency.
3.  **Index Out of Bounds**: If the mask is shorter than the `input_ids`, the attention mechanism may access out-of-bounds memory or ignore valid tokens.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
*   Any text-to-image model using a text encoder (CLIP, T5, etc.).
*   When implementing custom tokenizers or attention mechanisms.
*   When batching multiple prompts of different lengths.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
from transformers import CLIPTextModel, CLIPTokenizer

def encode_prompt(tokenizer, text_encoder, prompt: str, max_length: int, device: torch.device) -> dict:
    """
    Encodes a prompt with proper padding and attention mask.
    """
    # 1. Tokenize with padding to max_length
    inputs = tokenizer(
        prompt,
        max_length=max_length,
        padding="max_length",
        truncation=True,
        return_tensors="pt"
    )
    
    # 2. Move to device
    input_ids = inputs["input_ids"].to(device)
    attention_mask = inputs["attention_mask"].to(device)
    
    # 3. Encode
    with torch.no_grad():
        text_encoder_output = text_encoder(input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)
        prompt_embeds = text_encoder_output.last_hidden_state
    
    return {
        "prompt_embeds": prompt_embeds,
        "attention_mask": attention_mask
    }

# Usage in Transformer
def forward(self, hidden_states, encoder_hidden_states, attention_mask):
    # attention_mask is used in the cross-attention layers
    # to ignore padding tokens in encoder_hidden_states
    ...
```

**RULE**:
Systems exposing machine learning model definitions MUST physically isolate immutable tensor shape hyper-parameters (`config.json`) from mutable generation, sampling, and search policies (`generation_config.json`). Model loading routines MUST NOT mutate base structural configurations when dynamic generation strategies vary across execution contexts.

**WHY**:
Mixing dynamic inference parameters (such as `temperature`, `top_p`, `max_length`, `do_sample`) into structural model topology configurations causes serialization cross-talk and silent weight loader failures. When a multi-tenant serving pipeline updates generation parameters, dirty mutations written to a unified `config.json` can cause catastrophic state bleed across concurrent worker nodes, invalidating caching keys, or mutating runtime vocabulary offsets.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Apply to all deep learning serving architectures, LLM inference engines, model hubs, and serialization schemas where tensor dimensions ($d_{\text{model}}, L, H$) must remain immutable while inference request strategies change per query.

```python
class ModelStructuralConfig:
    vocab_size: int
    n_positions: int
    n_embd: int
    n_layer: int
    n_head: int
    activation_function: str

        self.generation_config = GenerationConfig.load(root_dir / "generation_config.json")
```

> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Autoregressive attention implementations MUST strictly prohibit bidirectional attention visibility by enforcing a lower triangular boolean/additive attention mask over non-causal indices. Under no circumstances may causal masks default to all-ones when padding or batch processing occurs.

**WHY**:
In decoder-only autoregressive language models, information leakage from future tokens ($t > i$) allows the model to trivialise the next-token prediction objective during training, causing the network to fail to generalize. At inference time, lacking an explicit causal mask causes outputs to collapse into self-referential token loops or degenerate semantic voids, because the attention mechanism attends to uninitialized or padding positions.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Applies to all multi-head attention implementations, custom CUDA kernels, causal language model evaluation loops, and speculative decoding pipelines.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch

def create_causal_additive_mask(seq_len: int, dtype: torch.dtype, device: torch.device) -> torch.Tensor:
    """
    Creates an upper-triangular masked attention bias matrix.
    Positions where mask == 0 remain unchanged (0.0).
    Positions where mask == 1 are forced to -inf.
    """
    # Create upper triangular indices (excluding diagonal)
    indices = torch.triu(torch.ones(seq_len, seq_len, device=device, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
    
    # Initialize zero tensor and fill masked positions with -inf
    mask = torch.zeros(seq_len, seq_len, dtype=dtype, device=device)
    mask.masked_fill_(indices, torch.finfo(dtype).min)
    return mask[None, None, :, :]  # Shape: [1, 1, seq_len, seq_len]

def causal_scaled_dot_product_attention(
    q: torch.Tensor,       # [B, H, S, D]
    k: torch.Tensor,       # [B, H, S, D]
    v: torch.Tensor,       # [B, H, S, D]
    causal_mask: torch.Tensor
) -> torch.Tensor:
    d_k = q.size(-1)
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (d_k ** 0.5)
    scores = scores + causal_mask
    attn_weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return torch.matmul(attn_weights, v)
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

    # LEAK: Allows sequence to attend to future tokens
    attn = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1) 
    return torch.matmul(attn, v)
```

```python
def test_causal_gradient_isolation():
    seq_len = 8
    q = torch.randn(1, 1, seq_len, 16, requires_grad=True)
    k = torch.randn(1, 1, seq_len, 16, requires_grad=True)
    v = torch.randn(1, 1, seq_len, 16, requires_grad=True)
    mask = create_causal_additive_mask(seq_len, q.dtype, q.device)
    
    out = causal_scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, mask)
    # Backprop from token 2
    loss = out[0, 0, 2, :].sum()
    loss.backward()
    
    # Tokens 3..7 must have zero gradient in query/key interactions for output at 2
    assert torch.all(q.grad[0, 0, 3:, :] == 0.0), "Future token query gradient leak detected!"
```

**RULE**:
Architectures relying on fixed, learned 1D positional embeddings (`wpe`) MUST assert that sequence length $S \le N_{\text{positions}}$ strictly prior to tensor indexing. Truncation or explicit error throwing MUST occur at the tensor boundary before invoking embedding table lookups.

**WHY**:
Unlike relative positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) which can extrapolate or scale via frequency adjustments, GPT-2 utilizes static learned embeddings of fixed shape $[N_{\text{positions}}, N_{\text{embd}}]$ (specifically $[1024, 768]$). Supplying an input sequence where $S > 1024$ triggers an uncatchable CUDA kernel assertion (`IndexError: index out of range in self`) or causes internal memory corruption if boundary checks are bypassed by compiled C++ extensions.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Every tokenization and forward-pass dispatch boundary consuming inputs for models with absolute learned positional embeddings.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SafeGPT2Embeddings(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size: int, n_positions: int, n_embd: int, dropout: float = 0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_positions = n_positions
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(n_positions, n_embd)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, input_ids: torch.Tensor, position_ids: torch.Tensor = None) -> torch.Tensor:
        seq_len = input_ids.size(-1)
        
        # INVARIANT: Strict Context Boundary Guard
        if seq_len > self.n_positions:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Sequence length {seq_len} exceeds maximum absolute position capacity "
                f"n_positions={self.n_positions}. Truncation or chunking required."
            )
            
        if position_ids is None:
            position_ids = torch.arange(0, seq_len, dtype=torch.long, device=input_ids.device)
            position_ids = position_ids.unsqueeze(0).expand_as(input_ids)
            
        if position_ids.max() >= self.n_positions:
            raise IndexError(
                f"Position ID {position_ids.max().item()} out of bounds for table of size {self.n_positions}"
            )

        token_embeds = self.wte(input_ids)
        pos_embeds = self.wpe(position_ids)
        return self.drop(token_embeds + pos_embeds)
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
