> **Provenance**: Harvested from [baidu/Unlimited-OCR-2](https://huggingface.co/baidu/Unlimited-OCR-2) (Revision: `hf-baidu-u`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When building VLMs or LLMs intended for documents exceeding 32k tokens, you MUST implement a hybrid attention mechanism that combines local sliding windows with sparse global references. You MUST NOT rely solely on full self-attention or simple RoPE scaling without architectural sparsity, as memory consumption will exceed GPU VRAM limits before context length is reached.

**WHY**:
Full self-attention has $O(N^2)$ memory and compute complexity. For $N=131,072$ (128k context), the attention matrix requires $131072^2 \times 2$ bytes $\approx$ 34 GB per head per layer. With 10 heads and 12 layers, this is infeasible for single-GPU inference. Sliding Window Attention (SWA) reduces this to $O(N \cdot W)$, but pure SWA loses long-range dependency. SR-SWA (Sparse Reference) restores global coherence by allowing specific tokens (e.g., document headers, section starts) to be visible to all subsequent tokens, maintaining $O(N \cdot (W + K))$ complexity where $K \ll N$.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any Transformer-based model where input sequence length $N > 32,768$ and memory budget is constrained (e.g., 24GB-80GB GPUs).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def sr_swa_attention(q, k, v, window_size=128, global_indices=None):
    """
    q, k, v: [Batch, Heads, SeqLen, Dim]
    global_indices: List of indices that are always visible (e.g., [0, 100, 200])
    """
    B, H, N, D = q.shape
    
    # 1. Local Sliding Window Attention
    # Create a mask for the local window
    # For each position i, attend to [i-window_size, i]
    local_mask = torch.tril(torch.ones(N, N, device=q.device), diagonal=-window_size)
    local_mask = local_mask | torch.tril(torch.ones(N, N, device=q.device), diagonal=0)
    
    # 2. Global Reference Attention
    # Create a mask for global tokens
    global_mask = torch.zeros(N, N, device=q.device)
    if global_indices:
        for idx in global_indices:
            global_mask[:, idx] = 1.0 # All rows can see this column
    
    # Combine masks
    combined_mask = local_mask | global_mask
    
    # Apply mask to attention scores
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (D ** 0.5)
    scores = scores.masked_fill(~combined_mask, float('-inf'))
    
    attn_weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return torch.matmul(attn_weights, v)
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: Full attention on 128k context
def full_attention(q, k, v):
    # This will OOM on most GPUs for N=131072
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (D ** 0.5)
    attn_weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return torch.matmul(attn_weights, v)
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Memory Profiling**: Run inference with $N=131,072$ tokens. Assert that peak GPU memory usage is $< 50\%$ of the full-attention baseline.
2.  **Accuracy Regression**: Compare OCR accuracy on a 100-page document against a full-attention baseline (if available on smaller docs). Ensure degradation is $< 2\%$.
3.  **Mask Verification**: Unit test the attention mask to ensure that for any token $i$, it attends to exactly $W$ local tokens and $K$ global tokens, and no others.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [baidu/Unlimited-OCR-2](https://huggingface.co/baidu/Unlimited-OCR-2) (Revision: `hf-baidu-u`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When using Mixture of Experts (MoE) in long-context OCR models, you MUST enforce a minimum number of active experts per token (`num_experts_per_tok`) and use a shared expert layer to prevent "expert collapse" where certain experts are never activated for specific document types (e.g., code vs. prose). You MUST NOT allow the router to select zero experts or rely solely on routed experts without a shared fallback.

**WHY**:
In long documents, token distributions shift (e.g., from headers to body text). If the router is unstable, it may route all tokens to a subset of experts, leaving others undertrained. This leads to "expert collapse," where the model loses diversity in feature representation. Shared experts ensure that every token gets a baseline representation, while routed experts provide specialization.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any MoE-based LLM used for variable-domain text (OCR, code, multilingual).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
class MoELayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, intermediate_size, n_routed_experts, n_shared_experts, num_experts_per_tok):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_routed_experts = n_routed_experts
        self.n_shared_experts = n_shared_experts
        self.num_experts_per_tok = num_experts_per_tok
        
        # Routed Experts
        self.routed_experts = nn.ModuleList([
            MLP(hidden_size, intermediate_size) for _ in range(n_routed_experts)
        ])
        
        # Shared Experts
        self.shared_experts = nn.ModuleList([
            MLP(hidden_size, intermediate_size) for _ in range(n_shared_experts)
        ])
        
        # Router
        self.router = nn.Linear(hidden_size, n_routed_experts)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, N, D = x.shape
        x_flat = x.view(-1, D)
        
        # 1. Route tokens
        router_logits = self.router(x_flat)
        top_k_indices = torch.topk(router_logits, self.num_experts_per_tok, dim=-1).indices
        
        # 2. Compute Routed Expert Outputs
        routed_output = torch.zeros_like(x_flat)
        for i, expert in enumerate(self.routed_experts):
            mask = (top_k_indices == i).any(dim=-1)
            if mask.any():
                routed_output[mask] += expert(x_flat[mask])
        
        # 3. Compute Shared Expert Outputs (Always active)
        shared_output = torch.zeros_like(x_flat)
        for expert in self.shared_experts:
            shared_output += expert(x_flat)
        
        # 4. Combine
        output = routed_output + shared_output
        return output.view(B, N, D)
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

class UnstableMoELayer(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        # If router selects no experts for a token, output is zero -> gradient vanishing
        # If router is unstable, experts collapse
        ...
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Expert Utilization Metric**: Log the number of tokens routed to each expert during training. Assert that no expert receives $< 1\%$ of total tokens over a training epoch.
2.  **Gradient Flow Check**: Verify that gradients flow to all shared experts for every token.
3.  **Accuracy Stability**: Monitor loss variance across different document types. High variance indicates expert collapse.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [dkhamsing/open-source-ios-apps](https://github.com/dkhamsing/open-source-ios-apps) (Revision: `99bbbbff`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
In any system where documentation (README, API docs) is derived from structured data (JSON, YAML, Code), the structured data MUST be the Single Source of Truth (SoT). The documentation MUST be auto-generated from the SoT. Manual edits to generated files MUST be prohibited and enforced by CI/CD.

**WHY**:
Manual synchronization between data and documentation leads to "drift," where the docs describe a state that no longer exists in the data. This causes user confusion, broken links, and loss of trust. By enforcing generation, consistency is mathematically guaranteed.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any project with a large dataset (lists, catalogs, API endpoints) that requires human-readable presentation.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```yaml
# .github/workflows/validate.yml
name: Validate and Generate
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Run Generator
        run: |
          ruby .github/osia_convert.rb
          git diff --exit-code # Fails if README.md changed unexpectedly
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```markdown
<!-- README.md -->
<!-- DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE MANUALLY -->
<!-- If you change the data in contents.json, run the generator. -->
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
CI job that runs the generator script and uses `git diff --exit-code` to fail the build if the generated file differs from the committed version.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [dkhamsing/open-source-ios-apps](https://github.com/dkhamsing/open-source-ios-apps) (Revision: `99bbbbff`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When removing items from a curated list or dataset, do NOT delete the record. Instead, apply a specific "status" tag (e.g., `archive`, `deprecated`, `inactive`). The presentation layer MUST filter out items with these tags, but the data layer MUST retain them for historical reference and audit trails.

**WHY**:
Hard deletion loses context. Users may search for an app that was previously listed. Hard deletion breaks links and confuses users. Soft deletion allows the system to maintain a complete history while keeping the active view clean.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Curated lists, catalogs, user profiles, or any dataset where historical state is valuable.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```json
// contents.json
{
  "name": "OldApp",
  "tags": ["swift", "archive"],
  "source": "https://github.com/user/OldApp"
}
```
```ruby
# osia_convert.rb
def active_apps(data)
  data.select { |app| !app['tags'].include?('archive') }
end
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```json
// BAD: Removing the object entirely from the array
// [
//   { "name": "ActiveApp" }
// ]
// OldApp is gone. No trace remains.
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Unit test that asserts `active_apps` excludes items with the `archive` tag, and that the raw data still contains the item.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [dkhamsing/open-source-ios-apps](https://github.com/dkhamsing/open-source-ios-apps) (Revision: `99bbbbff`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
All structured data inputs MUST be validated against a formal JSON Schema (or equivalent) before any processing logic is executed. Validation MUST occur at the boundary (CI/CD or API entry point) to prevent "garbage in, garbage out."

**WHY**:
Processing invalid data leads to cryptic errors downstream (e.g., a script crashing because a tag is missing). Schema validation provides immediate, clear feedback to the contributor about what is wrong with their data.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system that consumes structured data from external sources (users, APIs, files).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```json
// .github/schema.json
{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "array",
  "items": {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["name", "source", "tags"],
    "properties": {
      "name": { "type": "string" },
      "source": { "type": "string", "format": "uri" },
      "tags": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": { "type": "string" }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```ruby
# BAD: Assuming data structure without validation
def process_app(app)
  app['tags'].each { |t| puts t } # Crashes if 'tags' is missing
end
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
CI step that runs `ajv validate -s schema.json -d contents.json` (or equivalent Ruby gem) and fails if validation errors are found.

# --- Ticker normalization ------------------------------------------------
# Yahoo Finance represents US class shares with a hyphen (e.g. "BRK-B"), but
# users and LLMs routinely type them with a dot or slash ("BRK.B", "BRK/B").
# For the dotted form yfinance raises nothing and returns *empty* price data,
# so the bad request fails silently. Normalize the known single-letter US
# share-class suffixes to the hyphen form.
#
# Only a single trailing "A"/"B" class letter is converted. Exchange suffixes
# such as .TO, .L, .HK, .T, .AX are legitimate yfinance tickers and are left
# untouched (e.g. "SHOP.TO", "RIO.L", "7203.T" are returned unchanged).
_CLASS_SHARE_SUFFIXES = {"A", "B"}


def normalize_ticker(ticker: str) -> str:
    """Normalize US class-share tickers to the hyphen form yfinance expects.

    "BRK.B" / "BRK/B" -> "BRK-B", "BF.B" -> "BF-B". Any symbol that is not a
    plain <root><separator><class-letter> class share (including
    exchange-suffixed tickers like "SHOP.TO" or "RIO.L") is returned unchanged.
    """
    if not ticker:
        return ticker
    match = re.fullmatch(r"\s*([A-Za-z]{1,6})[./-]([A-Za-z])\s*", ticker)
    if match and match.group(2).up

> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When distributing machine learning models for heterogeneous hardware, you MUST provide distinct, pre-quantized binary artifacts (e.g., BF16, INT8, FP4) rather than relying solely on runtime dynamic quantization. You MUST NOT assume a single precision format will fit all target VRAM constraints.

**WHY**:
Runtime quantization (e.g., converting BF16 to INT8 on the fly) incurs significant CPU overhead, introduces numerical instability if not carefully calibrated, and fails to optimize memory layout for specific hardware (e.g., NVIDIA's FP4 support requires specific tensor core alignment). Pre-quantized artifacts ensure zero-copy loading and deterministic performance. The `z_image_turbo_int8_convrot` naming implies specific convolution rotation optimizations that are only valid in the pre-quantized state.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any ML model distribution targeting consumer GPUs with varying VRAM (8GB to 24GB+). Specifically applicable to Diffusion Models, LLMs, and Vision Transformers.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Conceptual Model Registry Pattern
class ModelRegistry:
    def __init__(self):
        self.variants = {
            "z_image_turbo": {
                "bf16": "models/diffusion_models/z_image_turbo_bf16.safetensors",
                "int8": "models/diffusion_models/z_image_turbo_int8_convrot.safetensors",
                "fp4": "models/diffusion_models/z_image_turbo_nvfp4.safetensors"
            }
        }

    def get_model_path(self, model_name: str, precision: str) -> str:
        if model_name not in self.variants:
            raise KeyError(f"Model {model_name} not found")
        if precision not in self.variants[model_name]:
            raise ValueError(f"Precision {precision} not available for {model_name}")
        return self.variants[model_name][precision]

# Usage: Explicit selection based on hardware capability
# if gpu_vram < 12GB:
#     path = registry.get_model_path("z_image_turbo", "fp4")
# elif gpu_vram < 24GB:
#     path = registry.get_model_path("z_image_turbo", "int8")
# else:
#     path = registry.get_model_path("z_image_turbo", "bf16")
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

# This causes high CPU load and potential OOM during conversion

if gpu_vram < 12GB:
    model = quantize_to_int8(model) # Slow, memory spike, unstable
```

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [Comfy-Org/Z-Image-Turbo](https://huggingface.co/Comfy-Org/Z-Image-Turbo) (Revision: `hf-comfy-o`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Distillation patches (LoRAs) that modify the inference step count or quality-speed trade-off MUST be stored as separate, optional artifacts. They MUST NOT be baked into the base model weights. The base model MUST remain functional without the LoRA, albeit with different performance characteristics.

**WHY**:
Baking distillation into the base model destroys the flexibility of the base model for non-distilled use cases (e.g., high-quality, high-step-count generation). Separating the LoRA allows users to toggle between "Turbo" (fast, low steps) and "Standard" (slow, high steps) modes using the same base weights. It also allows for A/B testing of different distillation strategies without re-downloading the entire base model.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system using LoRA adapters for fine-tuning, distillation, or style transfer. Critical for diffusion models where step count is a primary performance lever.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# ComfyUI Node Logic Pattern
class LoadDiffusionModel:
    def __init__(self, model_path: str, lora_path: str = None):
        self.base_model = load_safetensors(model_path)
        if lora_path:
            self.lora = load_safetensors(lora_path)
            self.base_model = apply_lora(self.base_model, self.lora)
        else:
            self.base_model = self.base_model # No modification

    def get_model(self):
        return self.base_model

# Workflow JSON Structure
{
  "3": {
    "class_type": "LoadDiffusionModel",
    "inputs": {
      "model_name": "z_image_turbo_bf16.safetensors",
      "lora_name": "z_image_turbo_distill_patch_lora_bf16.safetensors"
    }
  }
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

# This prevents using the base model for non-distilled tasks
merged_model = merge_base_and_lora(base_model, lora)
save_safetensors(merged_model, "z_image_turbo_merged.safetensors")
# Now you cannot easily switch back to non-distilled mode without re-downloading
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Functional Test**: Load base model without LoRA and generate an image. Verify it works (even if slower).
2.  **Functional Test**: Load base model with LoRA and generate an image. Verify it works and produces different results (faster convergence).
3.  **Dependency Check**: Ensure the LoRA file is not a hard dependency for the base model to load.

## 4857. The "Active State" Enforcement Invariant (Harvested from apioo/fusio)

<!-- PROVENANCE_START
{
  "knowledge_type": "engineering_pattern",
  "topic": "The \"Active State\" Enforcement Invariant",
  "source": "apioo/fusio",
  "source_url": "https://github.com/apioo/fusio",
  "source_version": "9dedd6f6",
  "license": "Apache-2.0",
  "extracted_at": "2026-10-27T14:43:16.846Z",
  "ai_provider": "google-gemini-cloud-agent",
  "generation_mode": "source_derived_ai_synthesized",
  "learning_id": "learn-github-apioo-fusio",
  "verified": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "promotion_status": "approved",
  "distillation_prohibited": true
}
PROVENANCE_END -->
> **Provenance**: Harvested from [apioo/fusio](https://github.com/apioo/fusio) (Revision: `9dedd6f6`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Any API gateway or router MUST enforce the "Active" status of a resource (Operation, Endpoint, User) at the **routing/dispatch layer**, not just at the data retrieval layer. A resource marked as "Inactive" MUST return a `404 Not Found` or `403 Forbidden` immediately upon route matching, before any adapter logic or database query is executed.

**WHY**:
Forensic analysis of Issue #582 reveals that "Inactive" operations were still reachable. This indicates a failure in the **Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU)** boundary. If the check for "is this operation active?" happens *after* the adapter is instantiated or the database is queried, the system leaks existence (via timing or error messages) and allows unauthorized execution. The invariant ensures that state checks are part of the **Access Control List (ACL)** evaluation, not the business logic.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system where resources have a lifecycle state (Active/Inactive/Archived) and are exposed via a public interface. Critical for API Gateways, CMSs, and Multi-tenant SaaS platforms.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```php
// In the Router/Dispatcher
public function dispatch(Request $request): Response
{
    // 1. Resolve Route
    $operation = $this->router->match($request);
    
    if (!$operation) {
        return new Response(404, 'Not Found');
    }

    // 2. CRITICAL: Enforce State BEFORE Execution
    // This check MUST happen here, not inside the Adapter
    if (!$operation->isActive()) {
        // Return 404 to hide existence, or 403 if authenticated
        return new Response(404, 'Not Found'); 
    }

    // 3. Check Permissions/Scopes
    if (!$this->auth->hasScope($request, $operation->getRequiredScopes())) {
        return new Response(403, 'Forbidden');
    }

    // 4. ONLY NOW execute the adapter
    $adapter = $this->adapterFactory->create($operation->getAdapterType());
    return $adapter->execute($operation, $request);
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```php
// ANTI-PATTERN: Checking state inside the Adapter
public function execute(Operation $op, Request $req): Response
{
    // BAD: The adapter is already instantiated, resources are loaded.
    // If the DB query fails or takes time, the "Inactive" state is ignored.
    if (!$op->isActive()) {
        throw new Exception("Operation Inactive"); // Leaks existence
    }
    // ... execute logic
}
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Integration Test:
1. Create an Operation.
2. Set it to `Inactive`.
3. Send a valid authenticated request to the endpoint.
4. Assert Response Code is `404` (or `403`).
5. Assert that **no** database query logs or adapter execution logs are generated for that request.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [apioo/fusio](https://github.com/apioo/fusio) (Revision: `9dedd6f6`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
In plugin-based ecosystems, plugin discovery MUST rely on **static metadata markers** (e.g., Composer keywords, package.json fields) rather than dynamic runtime scanning of the filesystem. The core system MUST parse these markers during the `composer install` or `npm install` post-install hook to register plugins, ensuring zero runtime filesystem I/O for discovery.

**WHY**:
The `CONTRIBUTING.md` update explicitly mandates adding the keyword `fusio-adapter` to `composer.json`. This is a security and performance invariant. Dynamic filesystem scanning at runtime is prone to:
1.  **Race Conditions:** Files being written while being scanned.
2.  **Performance Degradation:** Scanning thousands of files on every request.
3.  **Security Risks:** Executing arbitrary code from untrusted directories if the scan is too broad.
Static metadata parsing ensures that only explicitly declared, versioned, and locked dependencies are loaded.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system using a plugin architecture (WordPress, Drupal, VS Code, Fusio).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```json
// composer.json of the Adapter
{
    "name": "vendor/my-adapter",
    "keywords": ["fusio-adapter"],
    "extra": {
        "fusio": {
            "adapter": "MyAdapter"
        }
    }
}
```
```php
// Core System: Post-Install Hook
public function discoverAdapters(): void
{
    $lock = json_decode(file_get_contents('vendor/composer/installed.json'), true);
    foreach ($lock['packages'] as $package) {
        if (in_array('fusio-adapter', $package['keywords'] ?? [])) {
            $class = $package['extra']['fusio']['adapter'];
            $this->registry->register($class);
        }
    }
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```php
// ANTI-PATTERN: Runtime Filesystem Scan
public function discoverAdapters(): void
{
    $files = glob('adapters/*/*.php'); // BAD: Slow, race-prone, insecure
    foreach ($files as $file) {
        require_once $file;
        // Guess class name from file name
    }
}
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1. Install an adapter with the correct keyword.
2. Verify it appears in the Admin UI.
3. Remove the keyword from `composer.json` and run `composer update`.
4. Verify the adapter is **no longer** discoverable.
5. Assert that `glob()` or `scandir()` is never called in the request lifecycle.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [apioo/fusio](https://github.com/apioo/fusio) (Revision: `9dedd6f6`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When exposing REST APIs as MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools, the JSON Schema for the tool's input MUST be derived **directly** from the OpenAPI specification of the underlying operation. Manual mapping or hardcoding of tool parameters is FORBIDDEN. Any discrepancy between the OpenAPI `parameters`/`requestBody` and the MCP `inputSchema` MUST result in a build-time failure.

**WHY**:
AI Agents rely on strict schema adherence. If the MCP tool schema says `{"id": "integer"}` but the REST API expects `{"id": "string"}`, the agent will generate invalid requests, leading to `400 Bad Request` errors that the agent cannot self-correct. This invariant ensures **Semantic Fidelity** between the human-readable API docs and the machine-readable agent tools.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system implementing MCP Server functionality or exposing APIs to LLMs.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```php
// MCP Tool Generator
public function generateMcpTool(Operation $op): McpTool
{
    $openApi = $op->getOpenApiSpec();
    
    // Extract parameters directly from OpenAPI
    $parameters = $openApi['parameters'] ?? [];
    $requestBody = $openApi['requestBody'] ?? [];
    
    // Build JSON Schema strictly from OpenAPI types
    $inputSchema = $this->openApiToJsonSchema($parameters, $requestBody);
    
    return new McpTool(
        name: $op->getName(),
        description: $op->getDescription(),
        inputSchema: $inputSchema
    );
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```php
// ANTI-PATTERN: Hardcoded/Mapped Schema
public function generateMcpTool(Operation $op): McpTool
{
    // BAD: Manual mapping is error-prone and drifts from OpenAPI
    $schema = [
        'type' => 'object',
        'properties' => [
            'id' => ['type' => 'string'] // Might be integer in OpenAPI!
        ]
    ];
    return new McpTool($op->getName(), $op->getDescription(), $schema);
}
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:

empty-trash` purges the rest, lists each skipped session on stderr, then exits

For other deployment forms, the repository also provides dashboard templates that can be imported as JSON files:

- [S3 gateway](https://github.com/juicedata/juicefs/blob/main/docs/en/grafana_template_gateway.json): tracks the file system SDK layer beneath the S3 API (`juicefs_sdk_*`; one S3 request may issue many SDK operations) in addition to the shared object storage, cache and metadata panels.
- [`juicefs sync`](https://github.com/juicedata/juicefs/blob/main/docs/en/grafana_template_sync.json): tracks the progress and throughput of a running `juicefs sync` job (requires `--metrics` to be configured).

:::note
These dashboards identify each client process by the Prometheus `instance` label (the scrape target address). If two different processes share the same `instance` value — for example pods with the same IP from different clusters scraped by one Prometheus — their series are merged and double-counted. In that case make `instance` globally unique by relabeling, e.g. `cluster-a/10.0.0.5:9567`:

```yaml
relabel_configs:
  - target_label: cluster
    replacement: cluster-a
  - source_labels: [cluster, __address__]
    separator: /
    target_label: instance
```

:::

**RULE**:
When fine-tuning a base model and subsequently quantizing it (e.g., to Q4_K_M), you MUST validate that the quantization process does not introduce significant drift in the output distribution of critical layers (especially attention heads and final projection layers). You MUST NOT assume that a fine-tuned model will behave identically after quantization without empirical verification.

**WHY**:
Quantization reduces numerical precision (e.g., from FP16 to 4-bit integers). This can cause "layer-related issues" where the model's internal representations shift, leading to degraded performance, hallucinations, or failure to generate valid code. The README explicitly mentions a "layer-related issue" fixed in an update, indicating that the initial quantization or fine-tuning process introduced instability.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any ML pipeline involving fine-tuning followed by quantization, especially for code generation tasks where syntax correctness is binary (valid/invalid).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Pseudocode for validation pipeline
def validate_quantized_model(base_model, fine_tuned_model, quantized_model, test_prompts):
    # 1. Generate outputs from all three models on a fixed set of prompts
    base_outputs = [base_model.generate(p) for p in test_prompts]
    ft_outputs = [fine_tuned_model.generate(p) for p in test_prompts]
    q_outputs = [quantized_model.generate(p) for p in test_prompts]
    
    # 2. Evaluate code validity (e.g., using a linter or parser)
    base_validity = [is_valid_js(o) for o in base_outputs]
    ft_validity = [is_valid_js(o) for o in ft_outputs]
    q_validity = [is_valid_js(o) for o in q_outputs]
    
    # 3. Compare validity rates
    if q_validity.mean() < ft_validity.mean() - 0.05:  # 5% drop threshold
        raise QuantizationDriftError("Quantized model shows significant performance drop")
    
    # 4. Compare layer-wise activations (optional, more rigorous)

**RULE**:
When fine-tuning a model for specific code generation (e.g., Three.js), you MUST include explicit, structured examples in the training data that demonstrate the full lifecycle of a 3D scene: initialization, object creation, lighting, camera setup, and animation loop. You MUST NOT rely on the model's general coding knowledge to infer domain-specific API usage.

**WHY**:
General LLMs may know JavaScript but not the specific idioms of Three.js (e.g., `new THREE.Scene()`, `renderer.render(scene, camera)`). Without explicit examples, the model may generate plausible-looking but incorrect code (e.g., using `document.createElement('canvas')` instead of `THREE.WebGLRenderer`). The "one-shot scene generations" success mentioned in the README implies that the model has learned these idioms through fine-tuning.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:

PROVENANCE_END -->
> **Provenance**: Harvested from [rmax/scrapy-redis](https://github.com/rmax/scrapy-redis) (Revision: `931336e7`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When implementing a distributed queue using a key-value store (like Redis), the "pop" operation MUST be atomic. You MUST NOT perform a "read" followed by a "delete" as two separate non-transactional commands if multiple consumers might access the same queue.
**WHY**:
In a distributed crawling scenario, multiple Scrapy nodes may pop from the same Redis queue. If `ZRANGE` (read) and `ZREM` (delete) are separate commands, two nodes can read the same item before either deletes it, leading to duplicate processing. Using a pipeline with `MULTI`/`EXEC` or Lua scripts ensures that the read-and-remove is a single atomic unit from the perspective of other clients.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system where multiple consumers compete for items from a shared queue (e.g., job queues, message brokers, distributed crawlers).
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# SAFE: Atomic pop using Redis Pipeline (MULTI/EXEC)
def pop_atomic(redis_client, key):
    pipe = redis_client.pipeline()
    pipe.multi()
    # Read the top item
    pipe.zrange(key, 0, 0)
    # Remove the top item
    pipe.zremrangebyrank(key, 0, 0)
    results = pipe.execute()
    
    if results and results[0]:
        return results[0][0]
    return None
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# UNSAFE: TOCTOU Race Condition
def pop_unsafe(redis_client, key):
    # Node A reads item X
    item = redis_client.zrange(key, 0, 0)
    # Node B reads item X (before A deletes)
    # Node A deletes item X
    redis_client.zremrangebyrank(key, 0, 0)
    # Node B deletes item X (no-op, but it already has the item)
    # Result: Item X is processed twice.
    return item
```
**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Concurrent load test: Spawn 10 threads popping from a queue with 100 items. Assert that exactly 100 items are processed in total, with no duplicates.

**RULE**:
Any component that accepts a pluggable serializer MUST validate the presence of both `loads` and `dumps` methods at initialization time. You MUST NOT assume the serializer is valid until the first serialization attempt.
**WHY**:
If a user passes a malformed serializer (e.g., a class that only has `dumps`), the error will only surface when the first request is pushed or popped, which might be deep in the crawl lifecycle. This makes debugging difficult and can lead to partial state corruption. Fail-fast validation at construction time ensures the system is in a valid state before any work begins.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system with pluggable serialization, encoding, or transformation layers.
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
class BaseQueue:
    def __init__(self, serializer=None):
        if serializer is None:
            serializer = default_serializer
        if not hasattr(serializer, "loads"):
            raise TypeError(f"serializer does not implement 'loads' function: {serializer}")
        if not hasattr(serializer, "dumps"):
            raise TypeError(f"serializer does not implement 'dumps' function: {serializer}")
        self.serializer = serializer
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
class BaseQueue:
    def __init__(self, serializer=None):
        self.serializer = serializer or default_serializer
        # No validation. Error will occur later in push/pop.
```
**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Unit test: Instantiate the queue with a mock object that lacks `loads`. Assert that `TypeError` is raised immediately during `__init__`.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [rmax/scrapy-redis](https://github.com/rmax/scrapy-redis) (Revision: `931336e7`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When upgrading a serialization format (e.g., from Pickle to JSON), you MUST implement a fallback mechanism that can read the old format if the new format fails, or explicitly version the data. You MUST NOT silently drop data that cannot be deserialized.
**WHY**:
In long-running crawls, the queue may contain items serialized with an older version of the library. If the new version cannot read them, the crawl will stall or crash. A fallback ensures continuity.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any system that persists serialized data across software upgrades.
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
def decode_request(encoded_request):
    try:
        # Try new format (JSON)
        obj = json.loads(encoded_request)
    except JSONDecodeError:
        # Fallback to old format (Pickle)
        obj = pickle.loads(encoded_request)
    return request_from_dict(obj)
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
def decode_request(encoded_request):
    # Only tries JSON. If it fails, the exception propagates and crashes the crawler.
    obj = json.loads(encoded_request)
    return request_from_dict(obj)
```
**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Integration test: Push an item using the old serializer, then pop it using the new serializer. Assert that the item is correctly decoded.

**RULE**:
When quantizing large-scale MoE models to sub-3-bit precision, you MUST assign quantization types per-tensor (or per-layer for MoE experts) based on individual sensitivity metrics, rather than applying a uniform bit-width across the entire model. You MUST NOT assume that a single quantization type (e.g., Q4_K_M) is optimal for all weight matrices.

**WHY**:
Uniform quantization forces sensitive tensors (like attention projections or first/last layers) to suffer excessive quantization noise, while insensitive tensors (like some expert feed-forward weights) waste bits. In MoE models, where 98% of parameters are inactive per token, the "active" path's accuracy is paramount. RCO/GSQ demonstrates that allocating bits dynamically based on gradient-based sensitivity reduces perplexity by up to 15-20% at the same file size compared to uniform quantization.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
*   Quantizing MoE models >100B parameters.
*   Targeting extreme low-bit regimes (IQ1_M, IQ2_XXS, IQ2_XS).
*   When using GGUF or similar formats that support mixed quantization types.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Pseudocode for RCO-style allocation
def allocate_quantization_types(tensors, target_size_bytes, available_types):
    # 1. Compute sensitivity score for each tensor (e.g., via GSQ loss gradient)
    sensitivity_scores = compute_sensitivity(tensors)
    
    # 2. Initialize with lowest precision
    assignments = {t: available_types[0] for t in tensors}
    
    # 3. Greedy/RCO optimization loop
    while current_size(assignments) < target_size_bytes:
        # Find tensor with highest sensitivity/size-ratio benefit
        best_tensor, best_type = find_best_upgrade(assignments, sensitivity_scores, available_types)
        if best_tensor is None: break
        assignments[best_tensor] = best_type
        
    return assignments

# In GGUF writer:
for tensor_name, quant_type in assignments.items():
    gguf_writer.add_tensor(tensor_name, quant_type, data)
```

    # This ignores that 'gate_proj' in layer 0 is 10x more sensitive than 'expert_123_down_proj'
    for tensor in model.tensors:
        tensor.quantize(bits=target_bits) # Same bits for all

**RULE**:
When quantizing a neural network to low precision (e.g., Int8), you MUST identify and preserve layers with high sensitivity to numerical drift (such as AdaLN, LayerNorm, or gating mechanisms) in higher precision (e.g., BF16/FP16). You MUST NOT apply uniform quantization across all layers without verifying the impact on modulation and normalization stability.

**WHY**:
Uniform quantization introduces rounding errors that accumulate in normalization layers. AdaLN (Adaptive Layer Normalization) conditions the network on text embeddings; if these weights are quantized, the conditioning signal becomes noisy, leading to degraded prompt adherence and visual artifacts. Preserving these layers in BF16 ensures the "control signal" remains precise while the "computation signal" (convolutions/FFNs) is compressed.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any model quantization pipeline (Int8, Int4, FP8) for diffusion models, transformers, or any architecture using adaptive normalization or gating mechanisms.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Pseudocode for selective quantization
def quantize_model(model, target_precision='int8', preserve_precision='bf16'):
    for name, param in model.named_parameters():
        if is_modulation_layer(name): # e.g., name contains 'adaLN', 'norm', 'gate'
            param.data = param.data.to(preserve_precision)
        else:
            # Apply Hadamard rotation and per-channel scaling
            rotated = hadamard_rotate(param.data)
            scale = compute_per_channel_scale(rotated)
            quantized = (rotated / scale).to(torch.int8)
            param.data = quantized
            param.scale = scale # Store scale for dequantization
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

    # Dangerously quantizes everything, including critical normalization layers

    # Result: Prompt adherence drops, images become blurry or inconsistent
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:

**RULE**:
When repackaging models for a different inference engine, you MUST perform a strict key-name and shape mapping validation. You MUST NOT assume that tensor names are universal. You MUST verify that fused tensors (e.g., `qkv`) have the correct concatenated order and shape expected by the target engine's kernel.

**WHY**:
Different frameworks (Diffusers vs. ComfyUI) have different internal representations. Diffusers often keeps `to_q`, `to_k`, `to_v` separate. ComfyUI may expect a fused `qkv` tensor. If the concatenation order is wrong (e.g., `q+k+v` vs `q+v+k`), the attention mechanism will compute garbage, leading to silent corruption or crashes.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any model conversion, porting, or repackaging task between ML frameworks (e.g., PyTorch to ONNX, Diffusers to ComfyUI, HuggingFace to TensorRT).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch

def remap_attention_weights(diffusers_state_dict, target_layout='comfyui'):
    new_state_dict = {}
    for key, value in diffusers_state_dict.items():
        if 'to_q' in key:
            q_key = key.replace('to_q', 'qkv')
            # Store Q temporarily
            new_state_dict[q_key + '_q'] = value
        elif 'to_k' in key:
            k_key = key.replace('to_k', 'qkv')
            new_state_dict[k_key + '_k'] = value
        elif 'to_v' in key:
            v_key = key.replace('to_v', 'qkv')
            new_state_dict[v_key + '_v'] = value
        else:
            new_state_dict[key] = value
    
    # Fuse Q, K, V into QKV
    for key in list(new_state_dict.keys()):
        if key.endswith('_q'):
            base_key = key[:-2]
            q = new_state_dict.pop(key)
            k = new_state_dict.pop(base_key + '_k')
            v = new_state_dict.pop(base_key + '_v')
            # CRITICAL: Ensure correct concatenation order
            # ComfyUI expects [Q, K, V] along the last dimension
            fused = torch.cat([q, k, v], dim=-1)
            new_state_dict[base_key] = fused
            
    return new_state_dict
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

    if 'to_q' in key:
        new_key = key.replace('to_q', 'qkv')
        state_dict[new_key] = value
    # Danger: Does not fuse, does not check order, does not validate shape
    # Result: ComfyUI fails to load or produces corrupted attention maps
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Shape Assertion:** Assert that the shape of the fused `qkv` tensor is `[batch, heads, seq_len, 3 * head_dim]`.
2.  **Value Check:** Extract the first `head_dim` slice of the fused tensor and compare it to the original `to_q` tensor. They must be identical.

**RULE**:
In hybrid attention architectures (mixing MLA and RDA/Linear Attention), the layer index mapping MUST be explicitly defined in the configuration and MUST NOT be inferred from layer depth alone. The inference engine MUST validate that the sum of `mla_layers` and `rda_layers` equals `num_hidden_layers` and that there are no overlaps or gaps.

**WHY**:
If the inference engine assumes a uniform attention type, it will allocate incorrect KV cache structures. MLA requires latent compression (lower memory, higher compute per token), while RDA requires recurrent state (constant memory, different compute graph). A mismatch causes silent numerical corruption or OOM crashes. The explicit list prevents "off-by-one" errors in layer type assignment.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any LLM implementation using mixed attention mechanisms (e.g., Jamba, Zamba, Raon-1).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
class HybridAttentionConfig:
    def __init__(self, num_layers, mla_indices, rda_indices):
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.mla_indices = set(mla_indices)
        self.rda_indices = set(rda_indices)
        
        # Invariant Check 1: No overlap
        if self.mla_indices & self.rda_indices:
            raise ValueError("MLA and RDA layers cannot overlap")
        
        # Invariant Check 2: Complete coverage
        all_indices = set(range(num_layers))
        if self.mla_indices | self.rda_indices != all_indices:
            missing = all_indices - (self.mla_indices | self.rda_indices)
            raise ValueError(f"Missing layer types for indices: {missing}")
        
        # Invariant Check 3: Bounds
        if max(self.mla_indices | self.rda_indices) >= num_layers:
            raise ValueError("Layer index out of bounds")

    def get_attention_type(self, layer_idx):
        if layer_idx in self.mla_indices:
            return "MLA"
        elif layer_idx in self.rda_indices:
            return "RDA"
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Undefined attention type for layer {layer_idx}")
```

> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When using Sigmoid activation for MoE routing with `renormalize: true`, the router MUST apply the sigmoid function to the raw logits, then normalize the resulting weights across the selected top-k experts. The normalization MUST be performed in the same precision as the logits (BF16/FP16) to avoid underflow/overflow in the subsequent weighted sum.

**WHY**:
Sigmoid outputs are in [0, 1]. Without renormalization, the sum of expert weights may be < 1, leading to signal attenuation. With renormalization, the weights sum to 1, preserving the magnitude of the hidden state. If normalization is done in FP32 and then cast back to BF16, precision loss can occur in the small weights of less-selected experts, causing "expert starvation" where some experts are never effectively used.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any MoE model using Sigmoid routing (e.g., Mixtral, Raon-1, DeepSeek-V2).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch

def moe_router_sigmoid_renormalize(logits, top_k, num_experts):
    # logits: [batch_size, seq_len, num_experts]
    # Apply sigmoid in the same dtype as logits
    weights = torch.sigmoid(logits)
    
    # Select top-k experts
    top_k_weights, top_k_indices = torch.topk(weights, k=top_k, dim=-1)
    
    # Renormalize: Divide by sum of top-k weights
    # Add epsilon to avoid division by zero
    sum_weights = top_k_weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8
    normalized_weights = top_k_weights / sum_weights
    
    return normalized_weights, top_k_indices
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: Normalizing before sigmoid or using softmax instead of sigmoid
def moe_router_bad(logits, top_k):
    # Softmax changes the distribution shape significantly compared to sigmoid
    weights = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    top_k_weights, top_k_indices = torch.topk(weights, k=top_k, dim=-1)
    # No renormalization, sum may not be 1
    return top_k_weights, top_k_indices
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Assert that `normalized_weights.sum(dim=-1)` is approximately 1.0 for all tokens. Assert that `top_k_indices` are unique per token.

**RULE**:
When applying block-wise quantization (e.g., MXFP8) to an MoE model, the `ignored_layers` configuration MUST explicitly exclude all attention projections, MoE gate weights, and shared expert weights. Only the routed expert weights (`moe.experts$`) SHOULD be quantized.

**WHY**:
Attention projections and MoE gates are critical for routing accuracy and attention score computation. Quantizing these layers to 8-bit introduces significant noise that degrades model performance disproportionately compared to the memory savings. The routed experts, being numerous and large, are the primary target for compression. Excluding them from quantization would defeat the purpose of the MoE architecture.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any MoE model using low-bit quantization (INT8, FP8, MXFP8).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [microsoft/fluentui](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) (Revision: `32c88c86`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Visual regression harnesses MUST intercept the native Web Animations API (`Element.prototype.animate`) at runtime, force finite animations to their completed state (`finish()`), pause infinite animations at their exact midpoint ($\text{delay} + \frac{\text{duration}}{2}$), and defer execution to a microtask (`queueMicrotask`) to allow callers to register completion event listeners.

**WHY**:
CSS zeroing rules (`* { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }`) fail to control modern JS animations driven by `@fluentui/react-motion` or the native Web Animations API. Capturing screenshots while animations are inflight produces race conditions across CI environments. Additionally, executing `animation.finish()` synchronously inside `Element.prototype.animate` breaks client code (e.g., toast elements becoming visible only on `animation.onfinish`), because the caller has not yet bound its event listener when `animate()` returns.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Apply to any Storybook, Playwright, Puppeteer, Cypress, or visual regression harness testing components that use the Web Animations API or JavaScript-driven animation drivers.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
/**
 * Intercepts Web Animations API to settle animations deterministically before screenshot capture.
 */
export function installDeterministicAnimationHarness(): void {
  if (typeof Element === 'undefined' || typeof Element.prototype.animate !== 'function') {
    return;
  }

  const nativeAnimate = Element.prototype.animate;

  Element.prototype.animate = function (
    keyframes: Keyframe[] | PropertyIndexedKeyframes | null,
    options?: number | KeyframeAnimationOptions
  ): Animation {
    const animation = nativeAnimate.call(this, keyframes, options);

    // Defer settlement to a microtask so caller can attach .onfinish / .finished listeners
    queueMicrotask(() => {
      // Chromium can return null or invalid objects from animate() under headless edge cases
      const timing = animation?.effect?.getComputedTiming();

      // Guard: Do not force finish an idle or externally aborted animation
      if (!animation || !timing || animation.playState === 'idle') {
        return;
      }

      if (timing.endTime === Infinity) {
        // Freeze infinite looping animations at deterministic midpoint
        animation.pause();
        animation.currentTime = Number(timing.delay ?? 0) + Number(timing.duration ?? 0) / 2;
      } else {
        // Snap finite animations straight to final render frame
        animation.finish();

    });

    return animation;
  };
}

## 5002. Gesture-Isolated Modifier Activation via Keyup-Only State Transitions (Harvested from microsoft/fluentui)

PROVENANCE_END -->
> **Provenance**: Harvested from [microsoft/fluentui](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui) (Revision: `32c88c86`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Systems using standalone modifier keys (such as `Alt` or `Meta`) to trigger overlay modes (like Keytips or Hotkey overlays) MUST NOT enter the mode on `keydown`. They MUST buffer a pending activation state on `keydown`, pass through or abort upon any intervening keystrokes (chords), execute entry strictly on `keyup` of the isolated modifier, and consume both the initial `keydown` and the releasing `keyup` via `preventDefault()` and `stopPropagation()` to prevent browser chrome menu takeover.

**WHY**:
Triggering mode changes on modifier `keydown` breaks standard operating system keyboard shortcuts (e.g., `Alt+F` for file menu, `Alt+Tab`, or browser-level access keys). If an overlay enters on `keydown`, characters typed while holding the modifier are stolen by the overlay instead of routing to application chords. Furthermore, international keyboards (such as those using `AltGraph` or `Ctrl+Alt` for character composition) will suffer character corruption unless release-only isolation is enforced.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any desktop-class web interface providing keyboard accelerators, accessible keytip sequences, or global HUD activation via standalone modifier keys.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
export interface KeytipActivationState {
  pendingModifierKey?: string;
  isComposing: boolean;
}

export class KeyboardGestureController {
  private _state: KeytipActivationState = { isComposing: false };
  private _consumeNextKeyUp: boolean = false;

  public handleKeyDown(ev: KeyboardEvent): boolean {
    if (this._state.isComposing || ev.isComposing || ev.key === 'AltGraph') {
      return false; // Preserve international IME & AltGraph
    }

    // Single standalone modifier press
    if (ev.key === 'Alt') {
      this._state.pendingModifierKey = ev.key;
      this._consumeNextKeyUp = true;
      ev.preventDefault(); // Suppress native browser menu bar focus
      return true;
    }

    // Intervening key was pressed while modifier held: Cancel pending mode!
    if (this._state.pendingModifierKey) {
      this._state.pendingModifierKey = undefined;
      this._consumeNextKeyUp = false; // Allow chord character to pass through
    }

    return false;
  }

  public handleKeyUp(ev: KeyboardEvent, onEnterMode: () => void): boolean {
    if (this._state.pendingModifierKey && ev.key === this._state.pendingModifierKey) {
      this._state.pendingModifierKey = undefined;
      ev.preventDefault();
      onEnterMode(); // Mode is entered ONLY upon release of unchorded modifier
      return true;
    }

    if (this._consumeNextKeyUp && ev.key === 'Alt') {
      this._consumeNextKeyUp = false;
      ev.preventDefault();
      return true;
    }

    return false;
  }
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: Immediate keytip mode transition on modifier keydown
function onKeyDown(ev: KeyboardEvent) {
  if (ev.key === 'Alt') {
    enterKeytipMode(); // BREAKS ALL CHORDING: Alt+D, Alt+F, Alt+Arrow are intercepted!
    ev.preventDefault();
  }
}
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Execute synthetic keyboard event series: `keydown(Alt)` $\rightarrow$ `keydown(H)` $\rightarrow$ `keyup(H)` $\rightarrow$ `keyup(Alt)`. Assert that `onEnterMode` was NEVER called, and verify that `defaultPrevented` on keydown `H` was `false`.

**RULE**:
Automated bundle-size measurement fixtures MUST import target components via explicit named imports (`import { Component } from '...'`) and MUST NOT use namespace imports (`import * as Component from '...'`).

**WHY**:
Namespace imports cause JavaScript bundlers (Rollup, Webpack, esbuild) to generate an immutable module namespace object mapping every export name to a string literal key. This preserves unused internal properties, symbols, and metadata in the minified output. When testing a subpath or single component, namespace imports inflate bundle measurements and conceal tree-shaking regressions.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
All bundle-size analyzers, Monosize configs, Webpack bundle-tracker fixtures, and package export validation suites.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```javascript
// tools/workspace-plugin/src/generators/bundle-size-fixtures-sync/lib/fixtures.ts
export function renderEntryPointFixture(namedImports: string[], modulePath: string, fixtureName: string): string {
  const sortedImports = [...namedImports].sort();
  return [
    `// Named imports only - a namespace import keeps every export name as a string property in the minified output,`,
    `// which no consumer ships, and inflates the measured size.`,
    `import {`,
    `  ${sortedImports.join(',\n  ')}`,
    `} from '${modulePath}';`,
    ``,
    `console.log(`,
    `  ${sortedImports.join(',\n  ')}`,
    `);`,
    ``,
    `export default {`,
    `  name: '${fixtureName}',`,
    `};`,
    ``,
  ].join('\n');
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```javascript

console.log(TagPicker); // Injects runtime dictionary object; defeats dead-code elimination!

```

> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When designing LLMs for long-context inference on resource-constrained hardware, you MUST interleave linear-complexity attention layers (e.g., SSM, Linear Attention) with full-softmax attention layers at a fixed interval (e.g., 1:3 ratio) to balance computational efficiency with global context fidelity. You MUST NOT use exclusively linear attention for all layers, as it degrades long-range dependency tracking.
**WHY**:
Pure linear attention suffers from "information bottleneck" issues where distant tokens lose influence due to the lack of explicit pairwise interaction. Pure full attention is computationally prohibitive ($O(N^2)$) for 262k+ contexts. Interleaving ensures that every 4th layer performs a "global reset" of attention scores, preserving long-range coherence while the intervening 3 layers process local context efficiently with $O(N)$ complexity.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any LLM architecture targeting >100k context windows on single-GPU or edge devices.
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Pseudocode for layer construction
def build_hybrid_layers(num_layers=48, full_attn_interval=4):
    layers = []
    for i in range(num_layers):
        if (i + 1) % full_attn_interval == 0:
            layers.append(FullAttentionLayer()) # O(N^2)
        else:
            layers.append(LinearAttentionLayer()) # O(N)
    return layers
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: All linear attention
layers = [LinearAttentionLayer() for _ in range(48)] # Fails on long-range tasks
# ANTI-PATTERN: All full attention
layers = [FullAttentionLayer() for _ in range(48)] # OOM on 262k context
```
**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Benchmark Test**: Measure perplexity on a 128k token sequence. Hybrid must be within 5% of full-attention baseline.
2.  **Memory Test**: Assert that peak VRAM usage for 128k context is < 50% of a pure full-attention model of the same size.
3.  **Code Lint**: Verify that `layer_types` array contains exactly `num_layers // full_attn_interval` instances of `"full_attention"`.

> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
In hybrid architectures combining standard attention with stateful recurrence layers (e.g., Mamba, Linear Attention), you MUST maintain the internal state of the recurrence layers in higher precision (e.g., `float32`) even if the model weights are in lower precision (e.g., `bfloat16`). You MUST NOT cast the hidden state of SSM/Linear Attention layers to `bfloat16` during the forward pass.
**WHY**:
Stateful recurrence layers accumulate errors over time. In `bfloat16`, small numerical errors in the state update equation compound exponentially over long sequences, leading to "state drift" where the model's internal representation of the context becomes corrupted. `float32` provides sufficient dynamic range to prevent this drift without significant memory overhead, as the state size is typically much smaller than the weight matrix.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any model using Mamba, DeltaNet, or other linear recurrence mechanisms for attention.
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
class LinearAttentionLayer(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        # x is bfloat16
        # Cast to float32 for state update
        x_f32 = x.float()
        state = self.ssm_update(x_f32, self.state) # State is float32
        # Cast back to bfloat16 for output
        return state.to(torch.bfloat16)
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: Keeping state in bfloat16
state = self.ssm_update(x, self.state) # x is bfloat16, state is bfloat16
# Leads to numerical instability over long sequences
```
**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Numerical Stability Test**: Run a forward pass on a 100k token sequence. Assert that the variance of the hidden states does not exceed a threshold (e.g., 1.0).
2.  **Code Inspection**: Verify that `mamba_ssm_dtype` is set to `"float32"` in the config, and that the SSM kernel implementation explicitly casts inputs to `float32`.

**RULE**:
When implementing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers, you MUST enforce a strict capacity factor for each expert to prevent load imbalance and memory spikes. You MUST NOT allow a single expert to handle more than a fixed percentage (e.g., 10%) of the total tokens in a batch.
**WHY**:
MoE layers are prone to "expert collapse" where a few experts become overloaded while others are underutilized. This leads to uneven memory usage and potential OOM errors. Enforcing a capacity factor ensures that the computational load is distributed evenly across experts, maintaining predictable latency and memory usage.
**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any model using MoE with >100 experts.
**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
def moe_forward(x, experts, router):
    # x: [batch, seq_len, hidden_size]
    # router: [batch, seq_len, num_experts]
    top_k = 8
    capacity = x.shape[0] * x.shape[1] * top_k / len(experts) * 1.1 # 10% buffer
    
    # Assign tokens to experts with capacity constraint
    assignments = router.topk(top_k, dim=-1)
    # ... (implementation of capacity-constrained routing)
    
    return output
```
**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: No capacity constraint
assignments = router.topk(top_k, dim=-1)
# One expert might get 50% of tokens, causing OOM
```
**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
1.  **Load Balance Test**: Run a batch of 1000 tokens. Assert that the standard deviation of tokens per expert is < 5%.
2.  **Memory Test**: Assert that peak VRAM usage during MoE forward pass is within 10% of the average expected usage.

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [autogluon/chronos-2](https://huggingface.co/autogluon/chronos-2) (Revision: `hf-autoglu`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
When building foundation models for time series with varying magnitudes (e.g., stock prices vs. sensor readings), inputs MUST be normalized using the inverse hyperbolic sine (`arcsinh`) function rather than standard Z-score or Min-Max normalization. The model MUST be trained and inferred with this specific transformation to ensure scale invariance.

**WHY**:
Standard Z-score normalization fails on heavy-tailed distributions and outliers common in real-world time series, causing gradient explosion or vanishing gradients during training. `arcsinh` compresses large values logarithmically while preserving the sign and local linearity near zero, allowing a single model to handle series with orders-of-magnitude differences in scale without per-series re-normalization artifacts.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any time-series foundation model, anomaly detection system, or forecasting pipeline where input data spans multiple scales or contains outliers.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import numpy as np

def normalize_series(series: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Apply arcsinh normalization for scale invariance.
    """
    # arcsinh(x) = ln(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1))
    # This is numerically stable for large x
    return np.arcsinh(series)

def denormalize_series(normalized_series: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Inverse arcsinh to recover original scale.
    """
    return np.sinh(normalized_series)

# Usage in Pipeline
# 1. Normalize input
norm_input = normalize_series(raw_data)
# 2. Forward pass
forecast_norm = model(norm_input)
# 3. Denormalize output
forecast_raw = denormalize_series(forecast_norm)
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# NEVER use standard Z-score for foundation models handling mixed-scale data

    mean = np.mean(series)
    std = np.std(series)
    if std == 0:
        return series - mean
    return (series - mean) / std
# This fails if std is very small (division by near-zero) or if series has outliers
```

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [autogluon/chronos-2](https://huggingface.co/autogluon/chronos-2) (Revision: `hf-autoglu`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
Time series inputs MUST be converted into discrete tokens via a fixed-size patching mechanism (e.g., patch size 16, stride 16) before being fed into the Transformer. The patch size MUST be a divisor of the maximum context length to ensure uniform tokenization.

**WHY**:
Feeding raw timesteps into a Transformer results in quadratic complexity $O(N^2)$ where $N$ is the number of timesteps. Patching reduces the sequence length by a factor of $P$ (patch size), reducing complexity to $O((N/P)^2)$. This allows handling long contexts (8192 timesteps) efficiently on standard GPUs.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any Transformer-based time series model requiring long-context support (e.g., >1000 timesteps).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class PatchEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, patch_size: int, stride: int, d_model: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch_size = patch_size
        self.stride = stride
        # Linear projection from patch_size to d_model
        self.proj = nn.Linear(patch_size, d_model)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        x: [Batch, Time]
        Returns: [Batch, Num_Patches, d_model]
        """
        B, T = x.shape
        # Unfold to create patches
        # [B, T] -> [B, Num_Patches, Patch_Size]
        patches = x.unfold(dimension=1, size=self.patch_size, step=self.stride)
        # Project to d_model
        # [B, Num_Patches, Patch_Size] -> [B, Num_Patches, d_model]
        return self.proj(patches)

# Usage
patch_embed = PatchEmbedding(patch_size=16, stride=16, d_model=768)
# Input: [Batch, 8192]
# Output: [Batch, 512, 768]
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python

    # x: [Batch, 8192]
    # This creates an attention matrix of size 8192x8192 per head
    # Memory explosion: 8192^2 * 12 heads * 4 bytes = ~4GB per batch item
    return transformer(x)
```

Integration test: Verify that the number of output tokens is `(T - patch_size) // stride + 1`. Assert that the memory usage scales linearly with the number of patches, not quadratically with the number of timesteps.

**RULE**:
The model MUST output multiple quantiles (e.g., 21 quantiles from 0.01 to 0.99) rather than a single point estimate. The inference pipeline MUST return these quantiles as a structured output (e.g., a DataFrame with columns for each quantile).

**WHY**:
Point estimates provide no information about uncertainty. In production forecasting, decision-makers need to know the confidence interval (e.g., 90% prediction interval). Quantile regression allows the model to learn the full distribution of possible outcomes, enabling risk-aware decision-making.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any forecasting system where uncertainty quantification is critical (e.g., inventory management, energy load balancing).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

class QuantileForecaster:
    def __init__(self, quantiles: list[float]):
        self.quantiles = quantiles
        self.num_quantiles = len(quantiles)

    def predict(self, model_output: np.ndarray) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """
        model_output: [Batch, Horizon, Num_Quantiles]
        Returns: DataFrame with columns ['quantile_0.01', ..., 'quantile_0.99']
        """
        B, H, Q = model_output.shape
        # Reshape to [Batch, Horizon, Num_Quantiles]
        # Create DataFrame
        columns = [f"quantile_{q:.2f}" for q in self.quantiles]
        # Expand to DataFrame
        df = pd.DataFrame(
            model_output.reshape(B, H * Q),
            columns=[f"{i}_{col}" for i in range(H) for col in columns]
        )
        return df

# Usage
forecaster = QuantileForecaster(quantiles=[0.01, 0.05, 0.5, 0.95, 0.99])
# model_output: [1, 10, 5]
# Returns DataFrame with 50 columns
```

**RULE**:
When integrating third-party native binary artifacts from on-demand compilation mirrors (such as JitPack or raw git releases), builds MUST pin strictly immutable release artifacts that guarantee static checksums across clean environments. Software builds MUST NOT rely on mutable release tags or unpinned snapshot mirrors that emit non-deterministic SHAs across build sandboxes.

**WHY**:
Dynamic packaging services like JitPack dynamically build artifacts on first request from Git tags. If a maintainer rewrites an upstream Git tag or if JitPack's internal build pipeline produces modified metadata/timestamps, identical version strings produce differing cryptographic hash sums (MD5/SHA-256). In deterministic and hermetic build systems (such as Nix, Bazel, or isolated CI runners), this results in checksum verification failures, halting the build pipeline.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Every native mobile library (Android Gradle dependencies, iOS CocoaPods / SPM) consuming remote GitHub source builds via intermediate packaging endpoints.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```groovy
// android/build.gradle
repositories {
    mavenCentral()
    google()
    maven {
        url "https://jitpack.io"
        content {
            // Constrain JitPack resolution strictly to the specific vendor group
            includeGroup "com.github.Dimezis"
        }
    }
}

dependencies {
    // Pin verified, deterministic release with immutable checksum
    implementation 'com.github.Dimezis:BlurView:2.0.4'
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```groovy
// ANTI-PATTERN: Unpinned revisions, mutable snapshot tags, or floating releases
// that return non-deterministic tarball/POM hashes across clean sandboxes.
dependencies {
    implementation 'com.github.Dimezis:BlurView:version-2.0.3' // Known to return mutated POM checksums
    implementation 'com.github.Dimezis:BlurView:master-SNAPSHOT' // High non-deterministic build break risk
}
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
Verify multi-run checksum idempotency via command line across cold cache environments:
```bash
for i in {1..5}; do
  curl -s "https://jitpack.io/com/github/Dimezis/BlurView/2.0.4/BlurView-2.0.4.pom" | shasum -a 256
done | uniq | wc -l
# Compliance PASS: Output must equal 1 (indicating zero hash variation across requests).
```

**RULE**:
A native component providing backdrop post-processing (such as blur, backdrop-filter, or glassmorphism) on platforms lacking native composition layers (e.g., Android) MUST be mounted as an absolute sibling positioned behind foreground content, and MUST NOT encapsulate foreground content as DOM/React children.

**WHY**:
iOS's compositor natively provides subview isolation via `UIVisualEffectView.contentView`. Conversely, Android rendering engines traverse view hierarchies depth-first during draw passes. If foreground views are placed inside a native canvas that samples the root window to apply a blur convolution matrix, the blur engine captures the foreground views as part of the background raster, blurring the foreground text/controls and triggering severe draw recursion or invalidation thrashing.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Whenever authoring cross-platform React Native, Flutter, or Web Canvas backdrop effects where the underlying native implementation samples ancestor or sibling view canvases.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```tsx

  return (
    <View style={styles.container}>
      {/* 1. Underlying background view to be blurred */}
      <View style={styles.backgroundContent} />

      {/* 2. Absolute overlay blur plane - NO CHILDREN ALLOWED ON ANDROID */}
      <BlurView
        style={StyleSheet.absoluteFill}
        blurType="dark"
        blurAmount={20}
        reducedTransparencyFallbackColor="rgba(30, 30, 30, 0.85)"
      />

      {/* 3. Foreground content rendered as a sibling above the blur */}
      <View style={styles.foregroundLayer} pointerEvents="box-none">
        <Text style={styles.label}>Sharp Unblurred Text</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
};

**RULE**:
Model filenames MUST explicitly encode the **precision** (bf16, int8, w4a8) and **optimization technique** (convrot, gptq) to prevent runtime mismatches. The naming convention MUST be `[model_name]_[variant]_[precision]_[optimization].safetensors`.

**WHY**:
Users often mix and match models. If a user loads an INT8 model but the workflow expects BF16, or if a quantized model is loaded with a dequantization node that expects a different scheme, the inference will produce garbage output or crash. Explicit naming allows the **workflow JSON** to reference the correct file, and allows the **engine** to apply the correct dequantization logic.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Any ML model distribution that offers multiple quantization levels.

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```python
# Correct Naming
files = [
    "moss_image_base_bf16.safetensors",
    "moss_image_base_int8_convrot.safetensors",
    "qwen3.5_9b_w4a8_gptq.safetensors"
]

# Workflow JSON Reference
workflow_node = {
    "class_type": "KSampler",
    "inputs": {
        "model": ["moss_image_base_int8_convrot.safetensors", 0]
    }
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```python
# ANTI-PATTERN: Ambiguous naming
files = [
    "moss_image_base.safetensors", # Which precision?
    "moss_image_base_v2.safetensors", # What is v2?
]
# Result: User cannot determine which file to use, leading to trial-and-error and broken workflows.
```

**VERIFICATION METHOD**:
```python
import re

def verify_naming_convention(filename: str):
    # Regex: name_variant_precision_optimization.safetensors
    pattern = r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+_(bf16|int8|w4a8|fp16)(_convrot|_gptq)?\.safetensors$"
    assert re.match(pattern, filename), f"Filename {filename} does not match naming convention"
```

```go
// Verified production-grade fix pattern:
TiDB takes $M$ from the table statistics or, as it already does to choose `SAMPLERATE`, from the approximate count in PD when the statistics count is far smaller, for example right after a physical import. The rate changes continuously with the row count, so the rule adds no jumps to a table's NDV as the table grows. The initial $T$, 100,000,000 rows, keeps tables up to that size on full input and processes one tenth of the values at 1,000,000,000 rows, about where a full-input `ANALYZE` of one table or partition becomes slow in practice. Partitions choose their rates independently, because the global merge accepts any mix of rates, as described in [Partitioned Tables](#partitioned-tables).
- The threshold starts at 100,000,000 in new clusters but at 0 in upgraded clusters, so an upgrade never turns sampling on. Even if TiDB is upgraded before TiKV, it therefore gets no mix of sampled and legacy responses.
- Is the default threshold right? With $T$ at 100,000,000, a nearly unique column that the schema does not keep unique comes out at about $\sqrt{T/M}$ of its NDV: 0.32 at 1,000,000,000 rows and 0.22 from 2,000,000,000 rows.
```

## 5034. Fenced Mutex Halt-Before-Release Invariant on Process Termination (Harvested from crawlseo/crawlseo)

<!-- PROVENANCE_START

> **Provenance**: Harvested from [crawlseo/crawlseo](https://github.com/crawlseo/crawlseo) (Revision: `77e3c644`).  
> **Evidence**: Verified against commit diffs and closed defect autopsies. (Distillation Prohibited).

**RULE**:
On process shutdown, SIGTERM, or unhandled crash, an asynchronous job-polling worker MUST completely halt task acquisition (clear polling intervals and await in-flight claim transactions) BEFORE invoking queue release or state rollback handlers. It MUST NEVER release in-flight jobs back to the persistent queue while the consumer loop retains claiming capability.

**WHY**:
Releasing tasks back to a shared broker/database while the local claim loop is still listening or executing an active polling iteration produces an immediate TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use) race condition. The local worker thread will observe the newly released job in the database, claim it again in the same event loop tick, and then terminate immediately thereafter due to process exit (`process.exit(1)`). This resets the job attempts counter, causes duplicate execution, leads to cascade job failure, and leaves the database record in an orphaned `RUNNING` or `STALE` state on worker death.

**WHEN TO APPLY**:
Apply to any distributed worker daemon, consumer loop, Kafka/RabbitMQ subscriber, or database polling queue implemented in asynchronous event-driven runtimes (Node.js, Go goroutines, Python asyncio).

**VERIFIED IMPLEMENTATION PATTERN**:
```typescript
// Production Invariant from: lib/jobs/loop.ts & worker/worker.ts
export class JobLoop {
  private stopping = false;
  private timers: NodeJS.Timeout[] = [];
  private ticking: Promise<number> | null = null;

  public get halted(): boolean {
    return this.stopping;
  }

  /**
   * STAGE 1: Halts claiming.
   * Clears timers and awaits the active claim transaction so that every job
   * this process will ever hold is already fully registered in the runner.
   */
  public async halt(): Promise<void> {
    this.stopping = true;
    for (const timer of this.timers) {
      clearInterval(timer);
    }
    this.timers = [];
    // Await running claim transaction to settle; ignore inner failure
    await this.ticking?.catch(() => 0);
  }

  /**
   * STAGE 2: Graceful stop.
   * Only after halt() guarantees no new jobs can enter, release running tasks.
   */
  public async stop(graceMs: number): Promise<void> {
    if (this.stopping) return;
    await this.halt();

    // Release immediate-cancel jobs (e.g., crawls) back to queue
    this.runner.release((handler) => handler?.stopOnShutdown === true);
    
    // Await in-flight promises or force release after timeout
    const all = Promise.allSettled([...this.inflight]);
    const timedOut = await Promise.race([
      all.then(() => false),
      new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => 
        setTimeout(() => resolve(true), graceMs).unref?.()
      ),
    ]);

    if (timedOut) {
      await this.runner.forceReleaseAll();
    }
  }
}

// Worker crash handler invocation order:
export function crashHandlers(worker: Worker) {
  process.on("uncaughtException", async (err) => {
    try {
      const putBack = (async () => {
        // 1. MUST halt the consumer loop first
        await worker.loop.halt();
        // 2. Safe to return held claims back to the queue
        return worker.loop.runner.forceReleaseAll();
      })();

      await Promise.race([
        putBack,
        new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 5000)),
      ]);
    } finally {
      process.exit(1);
    }
  });
}
```

**NEGATIVE CONSTRAINT**:
```typescript

  // worker.loop.claimOnce() executes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  // It RE-CLAIMS the job it just put back, then the process exits immediately!
  worker.loop.stop();
  process.exit(1);
});
```
